The best accounts receivable software for your company is the layer that closes the stage where your cash leaks. If buyers settle from an emailed link and outreach starts late, a reminders tool covers most of it. If customers prefer to pay online by card or ACH, add a payments network with a customer portal. If clients require invoice uploads to Coupa or Ariba and clear multiple invoices with one blank-memo wire, you need an AR automation layer on top of the ERP. Every platform listed here serves B2B businesses invoicing other companies, excluding consumer payment apps and collection agencies.

Our source material is each vendor's public product, integration, security and pricing pages, plus G2 reviews, as they stood in November 2026.

About three in five US suppliers let business clients pay within 30 days, per Atradius's 2026 US payment practices survey (September 2026). Most overdue invoices settle within a month past due, so funds arrive roughly two months post-billing. The same survey notes US enterprises often lose 1% to 2% of B2B invoices to bad debt. Software that shortens this window performs four main functions:

What invoice-to-cash software does not handle is core billing operations. Billing schedules, revenue recognition, and GL accounting remain within the ERP. Contract-first platforms initiate workflows from signed agreements and map customer billing prior to collection efforts; invoice-first applications pick up after ERP invoice generation.

Most finance stacks have four layers: the ERP that creates the invoice and holds the books, a payments network, a reminders tool, and an AR automation layer working the steps in between.

The ERP covers the last row, and a reminders tool covers timing. The rows in between depend on reading what a customer or a portal sent, which is AR automation work. That share keeps growing. Paper checks fell to 26% of B2B payments in 2025, per the AFP 2025 Digital Payments Survey as reported by Nacha, and FedNow settled about 2.5 times as many payments in Q3 2026 as a year earlier, per Federal Reserve FedNow statistics. Heading into 2027, more money arrives over electronic rails while its remittance detail lands somewhere else.

On Xero or QuickBooks with customers paying from the emailed link, the leak tends to be timing, and a reminders tool covers it. Once W-9 requests and payment questions fill your team's week, the replies need a different layer.

Portal rejections and lump-sum wires put the leak in the table's middle rows, where an AR automation layer on the ERP fits. In a demo, we'd ask each vendor to show how fast its software flagged a rejected portal invoice, then to apply a multi-invoice wire with a blank memo live.

If your team still keys card numbers or chases ACH details, start with the payments layer. A payments network with a customer portal gives buyers stored methods and autopay. Unless the vendor says otherwise, it won't read replies or file into buyer portals, so plan an AR layer for those stages.

The Justice and Commerce Departments have announced an investigation into the company previously run by the woman officials have accused of being a Chinese spy while having an affair with Jensen Huang while he was Nvidia's CEO.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A criminal investigation into Megaspeed has been confirmed by the United States Justice and Commerce Departments, with a joint statement saying that they will “bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred.” Authorities believe that Megaspeed is one of a raft of companies that may have circumvented export rules designed to limit the sale of advanced AI chips, like those built by Nvidia, to approved companies and countries. The company is at the heart of the recent Jensen Huang scandal, which saw him resign from the company last week.

Megaspeed was added to Nvidia's no-sell list in June 2025, the statement reveals, but a New York Times report claims that a Malaysian Megaspeed subsidiary continued to receive large shipments of Nvidia chips for a full eight months after that date. It's believed that Nvidia's export-controlled Blackwell and H200 chips were shipped to Speedmatrix, either via third parties or directly from Nvidia itself, before being handed off to China. Nvidia has argued that it was given Commerce Department permission to ship the components to Megaspeed. Notably, Nvidia continues to list Megaspeed as a cloud partner.

The new criminal investigation follows a Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed that first kicked off in 2024 over possible export violations. By May 2025, it had requested Nvidia's data relating to sales it made to Megaspeed, and by June, officials visited Megaspeed and even interviewed Alice Huang, the now-former executive who is allegedly a Chinese spy. Ms. Huang is also the woman that then-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with before resigning his position earlier this month. Following that visit, the Justice Department took the lead in the investigation into Megaspeed.

Joint Statement from Department of Commerce and Department of Justice on Megaspeed Investigation. https://t.co/aAdtN9aDfFNovember 17, 2026

Megaspeed has long been accused of being a front for an AI component smuggling operation. In October 2025, an investigation claimed that it had helped move around $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips into China by importing them and then re-exporting them to the country. Megaspeed says that it complies with all laws and that the woman at the center of the affair scandal, Ms. Huang, is no longer at the company. The Chinese government has also dismissed claims that she was a state spy.

The joint Commerce and Justice Departments' statement pointed to its strong track record when prosecuting chip smugglers to date. 17 defendants across a total of six investigations have been charged so far, with more likely to follow. A Californian man was recently arrested after being accused of smuggling more than $300 million worth of export-restricted Nvidia chips to China. He now faces up to 20 years in prison.

Physical storage and memory are only getting more expensive, but that doesn’t mean we need to store any less. The alternative solution is a secure cloud storage platform, and there’s really only one good option.

That extends throughout every platform it’s available on, including Android, iOS, macOS, Windows, and Linux. On just about any platform, users get access to the pCloud Drive app for dedicated storage and backup. On Android and iOS, you have an additional option to automatically back up photos to free up space on your phone. pCloud Photos also acts as a smart photo gallery within the app, and sharing between other pCloud users and friends is made incredibly simple.

No matter where you access your pCloud Drive, all your files are there – safe and secure. You can store all kinds of files in pCloud, including documents, photos, videos, and even documents containing passwords.

Of course, you also get the option to take security a step further with pCloud Encryption. Your most sensitive files can be stored with an added layer of client-side, zero-knowledge encryption. The key is all yours, and no one else’s.

Even if you already have a hefty backup solution like an in-home NAS, pCloud is still a good option because it makes that NAS that much more useful. It has an official NAS backup feature with support for WebDAV, Rsync, SFTP, and SCP. pCloud simply provides another safety net for your existing backup.

Unlike a lot of cloud storage services, pCloud doesn’t charge on a monthly or even yearly basis. Just like buying physical storage, paying once for what you need is enough. But what makes it a better option than going the traditional route – beyond the skyrocketing storage prices – is the features and security that come with it.

#10404. New Gemini setting lets you keep chat history, but turn off AI training

Gemini’s existing Keep Activity setting “controls how long your chats are saved and whether they are used to train generative AI models.”

Google is now separating that preference into two new options.

This is huge. One of the major things Siri-AI users on iPhone like to point out is that while their assistant is a less capable portmanteau of Siri and Gemini, their queries are not used for AI training. Gemini on Android, on the other hand, offers the superior AI platform with the caveat that there is no way to opt out of training and still retain your chat history. Until now. Now users of Gemini on Android get the best of both worlds - the best of Google's AI models powering their AI experiences and their chat history siloed from AI training.

The first setting is called “History” and lets you “control how long your history is saved.” If disabled:

“…future chats will be saved for around 2 months and used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public, with help from human reviewers.”

The duration is currently 24 hours for chat context, and 72 hours to help protect Google, users, and the public.

The second setting allows you to “separately control whether your chat content, including text and attachments, is used to train generative AI models.”

With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.

If Keep Activity is currently off, the two “new settings will both be off.” These changes are rolling out over the “coming weeks,” and Google is notifying users via email.

The noose is tightening for Chinese AI labs that need U.S. AI GPUs to train their models.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

CNBC reports that Nvidia has started warning its customers that impending legislation to clamp down on countries accessing AI GPUs remotely via data center rentals could put them in trouble with U.S. authorities. Chinese tech companies could take advantage of the performance of American AI hardware through a loophole in U.S. regulations. Instead of importing Nvidia chips, which are under export controls, they instead look to data centers located abroad and export their data instead. This is what Chinese AI lab Moonshot is apparently trying in Europe, which is why the U.S. Department of Commerce, through the Bureau of Industry and Security [PDF], released an interim final rule closing this loophole.

According to the report, Nvidia has been messaging chip buyers to warn that RASA could expose both Nvidia and chip buyers to legal risk.

The U.S. House of Representatives has already passed a bill called the Remote Access Security Act (RASA) that addressed this specific loophole, but it’s been in limbo in the Senate for over ten months now. It remains unclear if the Jensen Huang affair and suspected espionage scandal will help speed up its approval, but scheduling could be tight with only about 31 calendar days remaining before the Senate's adjournment. But even before any of these regulations are approved and published, the company is already taking steps to protect its customers and has started requiring partners that 51% of their services should go to non-Chinese clients. It has also required its partners to join Nvidia’s Fleet Intelligence tracking system if they want to retain their official partner status

It’s unclear if these changes have been planned over time or were a reaction to the renewed scrutiny that Nvidia is facing. But even though Jensen Huang is now out of the company, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that it’s unclear if the former Nvidia CEO was aware of the alleged smuggling operations and instead laid the blame on the entire company. Nvidia itself has taken steps to improve its security and export control teams by establishing an oversight committee that will be in charge of its “national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risk management,” and would work with third-party experts in law, national security, and trade compliance.

These measures would further tighten the noose around China’s AI GPUs. Even though it has several domestic chip makers, many AI operators still prefer Nvidia chips for their performance and reliability. There have even been allegations that Alibaba and ByteDance, some of China’s biggest tech companies, prefer training their LLMs in Southeast Asia to bypass bans and restrictions. So, if the U.S. finally shuts down this loophole, we can expect these companies to scramble and find a replacement for the Nvidia GPUs they could access right now.

#10401. ‘We need to act now’: Senator plans AI hearings after tests discover these alarming national security risks

The incoming chair of the Senate Homeland Security Committee is preparing hearings on AI after government watchdogs found the four most-used platforms — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok — all created proposals for a terrorist attack in the U.S. when prompted by investigators.

Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., who will helm the panel in the new year, tasked the Government Accountability Office with investigating how commercially available AI could be used for malicious purposes, posing national security risks.

According to a report released Wednesday, the GAO found that within 12 hours of its covert testing, the platforms were able to create viable plans to use explosive devices for attacks with mass casualties in U.S. cities or to attack parts of the nation’s electrical grid to create economic harm.

“We need to act now,” Hassan said on a conference call with reporters.

The senator announced that one of the first hearings she will hold when the new Congress takes over in January will focus on AI risks and ways to improve safety.

“The AI public safety threat is no longer theoretical,” Hassan said in a statement. “If Congress does not act, it is a question of when — not if — a bad actor will use AI to plan and carry out a major attack.”

The 61-page report from the GAO includes responses from the tech companies — Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and SpaceXAI — who largely said they are continuing to refine their platforms to ensure security.

“The potential benefits of this technology are immense, but they can also benefit malicious actors,” the GAO wrote.

“As AI capabilities evolve, AI providers will continue to refine their safeguards,” the GAO said. “However, in its current state, this technology can potentially be dangerous and its misuse represents a growing risk to national and economic security.”

Government watchdogs conduct covert AI tests

GAO investigators conducted the performance audit from December 2025 to October 2026, including testing in the spring of 2026.

In response to prompts, two of the AI platforms produced plans for constructing and detonating an improvised explosive device (IED) to cause mass casualties, while two other platforms produced plans for using drones or firearms to target the electrical grid, the report said.

“Each of these platforms provided detailed information that could be used to carry out attacks, such as specific targets, locations, timing, and attack methods,” the GAO found. “Each platform took less than 12 hours to generate the attack plans.”

In one of the tests, the platform suggested renting a vehicle and picking up supplies from a store along a route to the location. It recommended a specific date and time of attack, the report said, because public events were scheduled anticipating large crowds.

While the GAO said the platform initially refused to comply with requests for detailed information about how to construct and detonate the explosive device, it said they were able to circumvent its guardrails and get the platform to provide the information.

The other tests had similar outcomes.

For the tests involving attacks on electrical substations, one of the platforms suggested a drone attack while the other suggested using firearms to attack substations near a U.S. airport — both designed to inflict economic harm. The platforms presented maps and images.

The GAO investigators consulted with experts and engaged in site visits to check out the accuracy of the plans provided by the AI platforms.

In one case, they noted that the roads were incorrectly placed, and in another, they noted the presence of high walls that would make it difficult to see the targets.

Tech companies say that AI models are evolving

In their responses to the GAO report, the major tech companies largely said their products continue to be refined.

Anthropic, in a letter to the GAO included in the report, said that it does not dispute that a determined tester can get harmful content out of an AI system by misrepresenting the purpose of a request, “and we take the finding seriously.” But it said it’s not able to verify the findings in the GAO’s report.

Google said the GAO’s testing occurred on earlier models, and “we continue to improve our models.”

OpenAI said it welcomes the opportunity to respond to GAO’s findings, “as well as the work that remains.”

SpaceXAI said it “continues to work diligently” to improve safety with each model release.

—Lisa Mascaro, AP Congressional Correspondent

#10400. Best Ecommerce Platforms for Developers: Six Options and the Layers Each Leaves to You

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Picking an ecommerce platform is really a decision about which layers you want to own: the storefront, the catalog and order logic, the payment flow, and the hosting underneath. Every platform below draws that line in a different place. If you have already settled the front-end question with a comparison like SitePoint's Astro vs Next.js guide, the next question is what sits behind it. Prices are from each vendor's pricing page as of November 2026

Shopify is the fully managed option. Basic costs $29 a month with card rates from 2.9% plus 30 cents, and a 2% fee applies to orders processed through a third-party gateway on that plan. Developers get two routes: Liquid themes, or Hydrogen, Shopify's headless toolkit, where your framework owns routing and rendering and Hydrogen supplies the Storefront API client and cart. Templates exist for React Router on Oxygen and for Next.js on Vercel. Plus starts at $2,300 a month.

Whop is a business platform for taking payments and sending payouts, and it sits under a storefront you have already built rather than replacing it. The Checkout element runs in the browser with no server code and no API key on the page. You pass your own order ID as metadata, Whop copies it onto the payment, and your server fulfills from a signed webhook that follows the Standard Webhooks spec. Domestic cards cost 2.7% plus 30 cents with no monthly fee, buyers see payment methods chosen by their location across 195 countries, and the same balance pays out in over 200 countries, including to affiliates or sellers you onboard. Whop's own guide shows how to integrate a checkout API into a Next.js storefront end to end. The trade-off is that there is no catalog or shipping engine; you collect address fields at checkout and trigger fulfillment from the webhook.

WooCommerce is a free plugin on WordPress you host yourself, so you own updates, security, and performance. Its payment gateway, WooPayments, charges US merchants 2.9% plus 30 cents per card transaction, 1.5% more for international cards, 2% for currency conversion, and $25 per dispute. Everything is PHP hooks and filters, which makes it the natural pick for agencies already living in WordPress and the wrong pick for anyone who does not want to run a server.

BigCommerce hosts the back end and lets you bring any front end. Core is $29 a month billed annually, capped at $30,000 in trailing annual sales, and plans auto-upgrade as volume grows. There are no platform fees when you use an embedded payment provider, and a 2% fee on Core if you use another one. Catalyst, its reference storefront, is built on Next.js, React Server Components, and the Storefront GraphQL API, and deploys to Vercel.

Medusa is an open-source commerce framework in Node.js and TypeScript, with an MIT-licensed core and a commercial enterprise edition. SitePoint covered it when it was still a young Shopify alternative; it now has over 37,000 GitHub stars. Self-hosting is free. Medusa Cloud starts at $29 a month for development, $99 for launch, and $299 for scale, with no percentage of sales, and the company says you can export your data and self-host at any point.

Saleor is a GraphQL-native, API-only commerce platform written in Python and released under the BSD-3 license. Self-hosting is free. Saleor Cloud starts at $1,599 a month for up to $200,000 in monthly sales, with 0.8% on orders above that, and $3,999 a month at the next tier. It is built for teams with a dedicated engineering function and a large catalog, which is exactly who should pay that price.

Own only the storefront, and Shopify or BigCommerce will carry the rest. Own everything, and Medusa or Saleor give you a back end you can read. Already on WordPress, and WooCommerce is the obvious fit. Already have a storefront in Next.js or Astro and only need the money to move, and Whop is the shortest path. Whichever you pick, the checkout is where disputes start, so log what SitePoint's friendly fraud guide for developers recommends from day one.

#10397. KFC store closures: See the full list of doomed restaurant locations as a large franchisee files for bankruptcy

Bad news for fried chicken fans.

Dozens of KFC restaurants have closed or will close their doors soon after their owner sought Chapter 11 protection this week—part of a wave of recent bankruptcies involving leveraged fast-food franchisees.

The franchisee, Tasty Chick’n LLC, operated 75 KFC restaurants and another nine cobranded KFC/Taco Bell locations across 10 states at the time of its bankruptcy petition.

But it also disclosed a list of more than 70 restaurants whose operations it did not deem worthy of continuing.

Those restaurants—many of which appear to have closed before the bankruptcy petition—are located in Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Missouri, Mississippi, Tennessee, and Virginia.

The Memphis area appears especially hard hit, with more than a dozen of the city’s KFC locations on the closure list.

Why did the franchisee file for bankruptcy?

Texas-based Tasty Chick’n and its affiliates say higher operating costs and declining revenue have eaten into their bottom line, with restaurant-level profitability declining since 2023. 

At the same time, the franchisee says costly demands for store upgrades from Yum Brands—parent company of KFC and Taco Bell—have led to $15.6 million in unpaid royalties owed to the restaurant giant.

The situation became so precarious that Yum Brands in September sent Tasty Chick’n a “notice of intent” to terminate the company’s franchise agreements, court filings say. The franchisee turned to the Chapter 11 process with the hope of selling its assets while it explores “other stand-alone restructuring alternatives.”

Reached for comment by Fast Company, a spokesperson for KFC said the brand works closely with its franchisees as they navigate difficult operating environments like this one.

“We’ve been actively engaged with Tasty Chick’n as it works through its challenges and remain focused on positioning our franchisees for long-term success,” KFC said in an emailed statement.

Tasty Chick’n did not immediately reply for a request for comment.

Which KFC restaurants have closed or are closing?

In court papers filed on Tuesday, Tasty Chick’n listed dozens of its restaurants that it says are closing soon, in the process of closing, or have already closed.

A cursory search of the addresses reveals that most of the stores are already marked as closed on Google, with some of the closures happening recently.

The company and its affiliates are now seeking court permission to get out of their lease obligations for the locations and abandon the properties.

Tasty Chick’n is managed by Tasty Restaurant Group (TRG), which oversees a sprawling empire of fast food restaurants across the South, Midwest, and Northeast—a fleet that includes Burger King, Pizza Hut, and Dunkin’ locations, in addition to KFC and Taco Bell. TRG is not identified as a debtor in the Chapter 11 proceedings.

Why does this sound familiar? 

Tasty Chick’n is not the first large fast-food restaurant operator to seek Chapter 11 protection this year.

In September, the owner of more than 300 Wendy’s restaurants filed for bankruptcy after years of sales struggles and a contentious relationship with the chain’s parent company. Franchisees for Denny’s, Subway, Moe’s Southwest Grill, and others have made similar moves.

Collectively, these franchisees have closed hundreds of restaurants in 2026.

Is KFC in trouble?

It’s not having the best year. Yum Brands recently reported a third-quarter decline of 6% for KFC’s U.S. sales. The picture is rosier elsewhere in the world, particularly in markets like the Middle East and Asia, where KFC’s Q3 sales were up by double digits.

The brand has faced increased competition in the market, particularly among younger consumers who have gravitated toward trendier chains such as Dave’s Hot Chicken and Raising Cane’s.

As of this writing, shares of Yum Brands Inc (NYSE: YUM) were up roughly 6.31% year to date, slightly underperforming the S&P 500, which was up 7.25% over the same period.

#10396. 105 major housing markets to enter 2027 above this key inventory threshold

Want more housing market stories from Lance Lambert’s ResiClub in your inbox? Subscribe to the ResiClub newsletter.

During the pandemic housing boom, housing demand was running so hot—and homes sold so quickly—listings barely even registered as active inventory. Indeed, in October 2021, there were only 565,707 active homes for sale, according to Realtor.com’s data series. That was a staggering 53.8% below the 1,208,311 active listings in October 2019.

At the end of October 2020 and October 2021, not a single one of America’s 200 largest metro-area housing markets had more inventory than in pre-pandemic October 2019.

Fast-forward to the end of October 2026, and there were 1,183,520 active homes for sale (just 2.1% below pre-pandemic 2019 levels)—and now 105 of the nation’s 200 largest housing markets have more active inventory than they did in pre-pandemic October 2019.

Among the nation’s 200 largest housing markets, the table below shows the 105 markets where active housing inventory for sale at the end of October 2026 exceeded the levels those respective markets had in October 2019.

While this data cut (active inventory in a market compared with the same month in pre-pandemic 2019) will slowly become less useful over time, it remains useful right now.

One of the common pushbacks I hear when comparing today’s active inventory for sale with 2019 levels is that some markets—like Tampa, Florida, and Colorado Springs, Colorado—have larger populations now than they did back in 2019. It’s true that some of the markets with higher inventory today compared with 2019 are also the ones that have experienced notable population growth in recent years.

However, that actual population growth—that is, a larger population base—isn’t the primary reason inventory has jumped so quickly in places like Tampa and Colorado Springs after the pandemic housing boom ended. Rather, it’s because those markets have experienced a sharper weakening in their for-sale market since the pandemic housing boom fizzled out, and that has helped push up unsold inventory in those markets.

This dynamic isn’t unusual. Growth markets that run hotter during housing booms often experience more pronounced cyclical cooling on the back end. As is often the case, stretched fundamentals, decelerated domestic migration, and elevated levels of new construction coming online—combined with an affordability-shifted market—collectively drive a larger supply-demand equilibrium shift.

That said, over time, changes in market size—specifically population and total households—will naturally affect what constitutes a “normal” level of active inventory in higher growth markets (like the Dallas metro area). By 2032, for example, comparing active inventory to 2019 levels will be far less meaningful than it has been in 2021 to 2026.

Because the “inventory compared with the same month in 2019” metric is slowly losing its usefulness, ResiClub has started using an inventory-per-1,000-household-residents cut (which we already keep in the ResiClub Terminal) for doing pre-pandemic 2018–2019 comparisons. For example, today we compared active inventory per household in October 2026 to the average between October 2018 and October 2019. Switching to this population adjustment to account for shifts in the base effect has some impact on the analysis and trend—but the general gist remains the same.

Note: This is NOT adjusted for sales volume. When looking at months of supply, you’ll find a far greater share of housing markets above 2019 months-of-supply levels.

Click here for a sortable version of the table below.

Generally speaking, housing markets where inventory (that is, active listings) has returned to pre-pandemic 2018-2019 levels (or exceeded) have experienced weaker home price growth (or outright declines) over the past 52 months. Conversely, housing markets where inventory remains far below pre-pandemic 2019 levels have, generally speaking, experienced stronger home price growth over the past 52 months.

Many of the softest housing markets over the past few years, where homebuyers have gained more leverage, are located in the South and Mountain West regions. These areas were among the nation’s top pandemic boomtowns, having experienced significant home price growth during the pandemic housing boom, which stretched housing fundamentals far beyond local income levels. When pandemic-fueled migration slowed and mortgage rates spiked, markets like Cape Coral, Florida, and Austin, Texas, faced challenges as they had to rely on local incomes to sustain frothy home prices.

The housing market softening in these areas was further accelerated by the abundance of new home supply in the pipeline across the Sunbelt. Builders are often more willing to reduce net effective prices or make other affordability adjustments to move product in a shifted market. Those adjustments in the new construction market then create an additional cooling effect on the resale market, as some buyers who might have opted for an existing home shift their focus to new homes where deals are still available.

In contrast, many Northeast and Midwest markets were less reliant on pandemic migration and have less new home construction in progress. With lower exposure to that demand shock, active inventory in these Midwest and Northeast regions has remained relatively tighter, keeping the advantage in the hands of home sellers (at least relatively speaking).

That said, as national active inventory continues to climb (up 7.6% year over year), some of the biggest year-over-year percentage gains of late have occurred in pockets of the Midwest and Northeast. To a degree, however, some of that is a base effect: Inventory in the Midwest and Northeast was so low recently that a given increase in listings produces a larger percentage gain than the same increase would in a Sunbelt market.

#10394. AMD attacks Nvidia's FP64 emulation at SC26, touts native double-precision on Instinct MI430X

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Reviews, benchmarks, and updates on current GPUs.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

AMD says Ozaki FP64 emulation is no replacement for the real thing when it's needed.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) opens in Chicago this week, AMD is indirectly needling Nvidia about the lack of native FP64 data type support in its data center GPU products. FP64, or double-precision floating-point math, is widely used in the high-performance scientific computing and simulation fields that are the focus of SC26. For those customers, AMD is trumpeting the value of its latest Instinct MI430X accelerator for customers that still need native FP64, like national laboratories and supercomputing centers.

Over the past few years, Nvidia has reallocated die area on its data center GPUs to favor the lower-precision matrix math that boosts the operations needed for much of modern AI inference. That reallocation only makes business sense, as the total addressable market for AI compute has exploded while the demand for double-precision math in large supercomputing installations has remained flat by comparison.

To make up for the lack of native FP64 support, Nvidia has turned to techniques that allow it to emulate FP64 operations using methods like the Ozaki schemes. But AMD claims this kind of emulation is nowhere close to a replacement for native double-precision processing for a few reasons—hence continued development of specialized products like the MI430X.

For one, AMD notes that Ozaki emulation assumes that the workload in question resembles a dense general matrix multiply (GEMM). In its own application profiling, the company says "less than 10%" of HPC workloads perform dense GEMM operations, so this emulation is a good replacement for native compute. Dense linear algebra is the one common workload for which AMD says Ozaki emulation is a natural fit.

For workloads like sparse iterative linear algebra, stencils and hydrodynamics, high-order finite element analysis, Monte Carlo and particle transport, and classical molecular dynamics, AMD says developers still need strong FP64 vector performance for the best results.

Furthermore, even for workloads that map well onto GEMM operations, AMD says matrix sizes must be large in order to achieve the best performance, and that might also not be a given for every operation. The operands of those matrices also have to be sized well to the hardware, as incorrectly scaled operands can reduce performance. The FP64 vector math capabilities of the MI430X are insensitive to those operand sizing issues.

Beyond those stumbling blocks, AMD also notes that using Ozaki emulation methods can cause the memory footprint of an application to balloon, requiring up to three times more capacity than native FP64 would.

Since HBM capacity is directly tied to GPUs in modern supercomputing installations, fitting a workload to a machine that can only emulate FP64 operations could have cascading effects on the number of GPUs and compute nodes required, causing knock-on challenges for the floor area, power, and cooling required to support the system.

AMD says the high 432GB of HBM4 memory capacity per MI430X node allows its customers to provision fewer GPUs and compute nodes in a system, saving on networking, power, and floor space.

In addition to its FP64 HPC performance, AMD positions an MI430X-powered supercomputer as an AI inference platform for developing workloads that utilize those models as part of the research process. But there are some key differences between those systems and the Helios rack-scale accelerator powered by MI455X GPUs from the same CDNA 5 architectural family.

Each MI430X GPU offers 9.2 PFLOPS of theoretical FP4 compute performance for inference, but that should be understood in the context of the whopping 40.3 PFLOPS of FP4 compute from each AI-focused MI455X accelerator.

Beyond raw performance, the native scale-up domain size of four MI430Xs over AMD’s Infinity Fabric interconnect when coupled with a sixth-generation EPYC host CPU pales in comparison to the domain size of 72 MI455X accelerators in a Helios rack. AMD says this interconnect is optimized more for latency-sensitive operations rather than a massive scale-up domain.

Of course, every customer and user of such a system will have different requirements, and institutional supercomputing installations usually aren’t trying to do double duty as cloud inference providers.

For scientists and engineers whose AI models of choice work well within the 1.72 TB of aggregate HBM4 capacity and 93.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth offered by four MI430X's working together across the 12.3 Tbps of scale-up bandwidth available within such a node, the inference performance of each node is likely more than up to the task of the kinds of AI applications that need to be run alongside double-precision compute workloads.

In any event, the MI430X can already count several supercomputing design wins in its corner. The upcoming Discovery supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, the Alice Recoque installation in France, the LUMI-AI system at Finland’s CSC, and the Herder system in Germany will all take advantage of the native FP64 support offered by the MI430X.

AMD’s continued support for native FP64, even as Nvidia retreats from that capability in its products, will doubtless be a point of pride for its architects and engineers, even as those institutional supercomputers will be dwarfed by both AMD and Nvidia-powered AI inference installations the world over. The company's semi-custom silicon design chops and chiplet experience give it the flexibility needed to tailor products like the MI430X to these specialized markets instead of pursuing a one-size-fits-all approach.

As the Senior Analyst, Graphics at Tom's Hardware, Jeff Kampman covers everything that has to do with graphics cards, gaming performance, and more. From integrated graphics processors to discrete graphics cards to the hyperscale installations powering our AI future, if it's got a GPU in it, Jeff is on it.

#10392. Grocery giant Aldi recalls tortelloni over potentially ‘life-threatening’ health risks: Avoid these products

Aldi has issued a recall due to the potential presence of Clostridium botulinum. 

Two tortellini products from the Illinois-based grocery store chain’s Priano brand might contain the life-threatening bacteria, according to a recall notice from Aldi that was reposted by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

Clostridium botulinum, or C. botulinum, can cause botulism, a very dangerous form of food poisoning.

According to the notice, the potential contamination resulted because the products may have been stored, distributed, or sold at improper temperatures.  

Here’s what you need to know about the Aldi recall. 

What products are affected?

The Aldi recall is for two types of its tortellini:

Priano Protein Carbonara Tortelloni, 9 oz, plastic unit 

  • Lot number: T9101926
  • Best-by date: December 18, 2026

Priano Protein Herb & Cheese Tortelloni, 9 oz, plastic unit

  • Lot number: T9101926
  • Best-by date: December 18, 2026

Where and when was the product sold?

The announcement doesn’t say exactly when the tortellini products were sold, but we do know where. Aldi sold the recalled products in-store and online from stores in the following states:

  • Alabama
  • Georgia
  • North Carolina 
  • South Carolina

What should I do if I have this product? 

You should either throw out the recalled tortellini or return it to Aldi for a full refund. “Consumers are warned not to prepare or consume the affected products from the impacted states, even if they do not look or smell spoiled,” the announcement states.

You can contact Aldi with any questions at (844) 484-0332 from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. ET, Monday to Friday. 

What botulism signs should I look out for? 

Get medical attention immediately if you’ve eaten the recalled tortellini and experience any of the following symptoms of botulism: 

  • Abdominal distension
  • Constipation
  • Difficulty breathing
  • Dizziness
  • Double vision
  • General weakness
  • Muscle weakness
  • Trouble speaking or swallowing

#10391. Jensen’s exit could be Google’s TPU moment

Good morning. Today I’m rewatching Tenet to better picture Robert Pattinson in his new role, sighing over the inevitability of delivery drones triggering PTSD symptoms, and laugh-cringing at some of these Bit.ly link hijack stories from the weekend. Plus, prayers to anyone who had to find a last-minute hotel room during last week’s flying nightmare.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

In the immediate fallout of Jensen Huang’s humiliating resignation from Nvidia, coverage will focus on how the company plans to continue without its beloved former CEO, the world’s biggest champion of open-source AI and the proliferation of GPUs across borders. But in the long term, there’s an argument to be made that Google will be one of the largest winners of the shake-up, with a market opening up to competition outside of Nvidia’s CUDA moat.

While Colette Kress, the interim CEO, is unlikely to make any drastic changes to the company’s roadmap, the reality is that Nvidia’s competitors in the semiconductor space have desperately been working to unseat the market leader, and without Jensen at the helm, customers may be more likely to pursue alternatives.

For years, Google has offered its TPUs, or Tensor Processing Units, as a solution for AI training and inference, but they’ve been largely locked to its Google Cloud infrastructure. That’s changing now that the company is opening up sales to third parties and has announced it will bring TPU capacity to Oracle’s cloud beginning in 2027.

Google’s latest generation of TPUs is specialized; here’s how the company describes the lineup in its recent announcement post:

While flexible across workloads, together the four systems in our eighth-generation TPUs give customers a purpose-built accelerator for every stage of the agentic lifecycle. TPU 8t for scale-up training, TPU 8i for low-latency reasoning (inference), TPU 8tx for confidential computing, and TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack.

Google isn’t comparing its new TPUs directly to Nvidia’s offerings, and clock-for-clock, even the most powerful TPU 8i Max doesn’t touch Vera Rubin for sheer performance. But this generation should be much more competitive for a few reasons: it’s more power efficient in certain configurations, and Google made it easier to translate coding workflows optimized for CUDA to work with its TPUs.

Back in October, Google open-sourced TorchTPU, which it co-developed with Meta’s PyTorch team, to let developers use familiar PyTorch workflows on TPUs with minimal code changes. That won’t make every custom CUDA operation portable or eliminate performance tuning, but reducing the effort required to try an alternative may change the buying decision. Customers don’t need to abandon Nvidia outright for Google to increase its TPU market share, or for Nvidia to face more pressure on price.

Alongside Broadcom and MediaTek, Google is taking on the Nvidia behemoth, and in the short term, it will almost certainly see a large upside in sentiment. But in the longer term, with scaling pressure lowering margins for Nvidia, Google’s specialized and more efficient TPUs may be a primary beneficiary of this sea change. They could also offset a slowdown in Search as Google’s shift to Cloud continues apace.

#10390. Don’t get distracted by apps—the true power of AI is systems thinking

In the spring of 1893, a 24-year-old engineer named William Henry Merrill arrived in Chicago with an unglamorous assignment. The World’s Columbian Exposition was about to show off electric light on a scale nobody had seen, with more than 100,000 incandescent lamps. There was just one little problem — the new technology was not only new, it was dangerous, and fires kept breaking out unexpectedly. 

Merrill realized that to become truly useful, the electricity system would have to be designed as, well, a system. The following year he ran his first product test in a small lab above a Chicago fire patrol station. That lab became Underwriters Laboratories, and it was instrumental in creating system-wide standards. By 1897, insurers, engineers, and the electrical industry had agreed on the first National Electrical Code.

Neither the lab nor the code produced a single watt of power. But electricity could not have fundamentally transformed our lives without them.

I’ve been thinking about Merrill since a recent conversation with Leigh-Ann Russell, the chief technology officer and global head of engineering at BNY, America’s oldest bank. Russell is a mechanical engineer who spent 18 years at BP before moving into banking, and she brought some of the energy industry’s vocabulary with her. One word in particular has stayed with me: interlock.

The device that says no

An interlock stops a system from operating until the conditions for operating it safely have been met. Railways developed the idea so that signals and switches could not be set against each other. In 1922, with London electrifying and switchgear injuring and killing the people who worked on it, an engineer named James Harry Castell borrowed the concept from the railways. In his design, the key that opens an equipment cabinet stays trapped in the switch for as long as the power is on. Nobody has to remember the rule, because the hardware won’t allow anything else.

Shipping learned the same lesson at a terrible price. In March 1987 the ferry Herald of Free Enterprise left Zeebrugge with its bow doors open and capsized, killing 193 people. The doors could not be seen from the bridge and there was no indicator light, although captains had asked for one. Just over a year later, international regulators adopted a rule requiring door indicators on the bridge.

Russell’s point is that industries like these do not wait until the plant is running to ask what happens when one component misbehaves. And they never assume that because every part works, the whole will.

“It’s clear to me that there is a generational opportunity taking place right now with AI and, like other transformational technology before it, the early innings are critical. However, there will be many inflection points. Phase one was adoption and now we’re moving to adaption. To engineering a system that both compounds in value over time but also reinvents itself,” Russell said. “To me, this is the moment to be principled about what we build, who it benefits, but most critically how it builds trust.”

Edison’s real invention

What Thomas Edison switched on at Pearl Street in lower Manhattan on September 4, 1882, was a complete system: dynamos, 80,000 feet of underground conductors, switches, sockets, meters to bill customers, and safety fuses to keep a fault in one building from becoming a fire in the next. His team had to design most of it because none of it existed. The historian Thomas Hughes built a classic study, Networks of Power, around this observation: Edison’s achievement was the system.

Even with the system in place, the payoff was slow. The economist Paul David showed that by 1899, almost two decades after Pearl Street, electric motors supplied less than 5% of the mechanical drives in American factories. Owners who did electrify usually swapped the steam engine for one large motor and left the shafts and belts where they were. The productivity surge came in the 1920s, once factories were redesigned around a small motor on every machine.

Which brings us to where we are with AI. Most organizations are in the swap-the-engine phase with AI. Models are better, code is cheap, and a team can prototype in an afternoon what used to take a quarter. So one team builds an agent, another deploys a chatbot, a third pilots a workflow tool. Each is clever and locally useful. Together they add up to fragmented workflows, inconsistent controls, duplicated costs, new security exposure, and a technology estate that someone has to run. Gartner predicts that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, and the reasons it gives are escalating costs, unclear business value, and inadequate risk controls.

Four disciplines, wired together

Russell says that for years she has asked the same questions of any growth opportunity: Will customers love it? Can we build it? Will it create value? Does it survive in the broader ecosystem, or is it a point solution? With AI, she argues, an application can pass all four and still leave the organization more expensive, more fragile, and harder to govern. So she adds a fifth: Can we build and operate it safely as part of a larger system?

Her answer is to design governance, security, verification, and observability into the architecture from the start, and she organizes that work around four disciplines.

Intent. Start with a real problem. When building gets cheap, deciding what not to build becomes more valuable.

Integrity. Engineer trust into the system: clear boundaries, meaningful evaluation, visibility into behavior, and working mechanisms for a human to step in. I think of this as the AI equivalent of the fuse box.

Infrastructure. Which model is best matters less than the layers around it: data, integration, compute, controls, and monitoring. Shared, reusable foundations beat a collection of bespoke wins. This is the equivalent of a safe distribution system.

Impact. Ask what changed. Did customers get a better experience? Did productivity improve? Did risk go down? Did the benefits cover the full cost of integrating, operating, and governing the thing? This is the AI version of the meter. Edison had to invent that too.

What makes this an interlock and not a checklist is that the four depend on one another. Intent shapes the infrastructure. Infrastructure makes integrity practical. Integrity is what allows responsible deployment, and impact tells you whether the original intent was sound.

What leaders should take from this

Count systems, not demos. Building something visible has never been cheaper, which makes visible activity a poor measure of progress. The better question is whether each new tool makes a contribution to the whole, not just to an isolated problem.

Treat governance as engineering. Nobody regards a circuit breaker as useless bureaucracy. The electrical code is the reason you can plug an appliance into an outlet without thinking about it. Shared AI foundations should do the same job, so that each new use case is faster to deploy and cheaper to operate because the hard parts are already designed and instrumented.

Measure the whole. A use case that succeeds locally can impose costs elsewhere. Judge AI by what it does to the full operating model.

Leave room to rewire. The factories that won in the 1920s could rearrange their floors as demand changed. An AI architecture so tightly coupled that one change forces a rebuild of everything else will not age well.

We have spent the past few years asking what AI can do. Russell thinks the next questions are harder: What should we build, how should we engineer it, how do we operate it safely, and how will we know it was worth doing?

Nobody remembers which exhibitor had the brightest lamps in Chicago in 1893. The electrical code that came out of that decade is still being revised and enforced today. Merrill’s motto was “Know by test, and state the facts,” and it would serve an AI program well.

A page can return 200 OK, exist in an XML sitemap, and still be practically invisible to anyone browsing the site.

You do not need a full commercial crawler to find the obvious cases. A small Node.js script can compare two things:

Anything present in the first set but missing from the second deserves investigation.

You now have URLs that the application publishes through its sitemap but that your HTML crawl could not reach.

The page might be intentionally isolated. It might exist for a campaign. Navigation might depend on JavaScript. Your crawler may have missed authentication or pagination.

Should a normal visitor reasonably be able to discover this page from another page on the site?

Google recommends using standard crawlable elements with resolvable href values for links that should be discoverable. Google's guidance on crawlable links

That is also good web architecture independent of SEO.

Internal links should not exist merely to move ranking signals around.

They should help users move between related tasks.

A technical guide might lead to a product page. A product page might link back to the configuration guide. A category page should make important child resources discoverable without requiring a user to know the exact URL.

This is why on-page SEO and internal linking are closely connected to site architecture. Good internal links clarify relationships for both visitors and crawlers.

At a broader level, crawlability is one part of technical SEO and search visibility. A page that nobody can reliably discover is difficult to evaluate regardless of how strong its content may be.

If an important URL appears disconnected because navigation is created only after client-side JavaScript runs, the script has surfaced a real architectural fact.

You can then decide whether that is acceptable.

If your application genuinely requires rendered-DOM crawling, replace the fetch-and-Cheerio layer with Playwright.

Do not make the simple crawler pretend to be something it is not.

The best output from this tool is not an "SEO score."

It is a concrete question for the development team:

This page exists. The sitemap knows about it. Why can't a normal HTML crawl reach it?

Similar to a recent iPhone feature, Google appears to be working on “Fast Switch” as a way to share one SIM and phone number on two Android phones at once, and it sounds pretty cool.

Through the SIM Manager app on Android, the folks over at Android Authority noticed strings that tell a pretty clear story.

A new feature called “Android Fast Switch” would let you “use your phone number on up to two phones,” with the SIM automatically switching to “whichever phone you unlock.”

“Android Fast Switch” sounds nearly identical to Handoff on iPhone, a feature that lets iPhone owners share one SIM between two iPhones and quickly switch devices on the fly.

Other strings explicitly say that you can “Use a SIM on two phones” and specify that both devices would need to be logged into the same Google account. One phone would be the “Primary” with the other as a “companion.”

On iPhone, carriers either charge extra for this feature ($5 at T-Mobile, $10 at Verizon), or don’t support it at all (AT&T). We also don’t know what devices may be supported – this could easily end up as a Pixel-only affair.

This would make my decision to buy device like Clicks Communicator much easier

As per usual with these early teardowns, though, the actual launch of a feature like this could be weeks, months, or even years away. Still, the idea itself is rather exciting.

iPhone’s Handoff feature always sounded useful, but I personally always questioned why it would be useful on iPhone. With so little variety in hardware, the utility of switching between two iPhones seems somewhat dubious, outside of perhaps using a Mini or Air as a situational device alongside a Pro device.

On Android, the combinations are endless. It all just depends on what devices Google supports. What devices would you switch between?

#10385. Marc Andreessen has a surprisingly mundane prediction about AI’s impact

When it comes to AI’s potential impact on the economy, Marc Andreessen thinks extreme optimists and extreme pessimists have one thing in common: they are both wrong.  

“Both the utopians and the doomers are going to be disappointed [by] the scope and magnitude of the real-world impact [of AI], and specifically the economic impact,” the prominent venture capitalist said Monday at the Federal Reserve’s AI conference in San Francisco.

Andreessen thinks both camps are overlooking that vast economic sectors—including health care, education, housing, law, and government—are blocked from rapid transformation by heavy regulation, limited competition, and other factors.

While this could limit AI-driven job losses in those sectors, it could also make their services increasingly expensive relative to other goods and services.

“[Health care] is already a fifth of U.S. GDP, and I don’t see why it doesn’t go to a fourth, a third and then half and then ultimately 80%,” Andreessen said.

The implications of this view depend on your values, he added.  

“You might interpret this as good news, because it means the AI revolution is not going to, you know, destroy all the jobs or kill everybody,” he said. “You could also view this as very negative, which is [that] productivity … simply may not grow very much.”

Andreessen is the co-founder and general partner of Silicon Valley venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz and co-leader of Fed chairman Kevin Warsh’s Productivity and Jobs Task Force.

Andreessen’s comments on Monday marked a change in tone, if not substance, from many of his previous remarks on AI. 

In 2023, he famously argued that “AI will save the world” and that “productivity growth throughout the economy will accelerate dramatically”—leading to higher wages, lower prices and more jobs.

Andreessen has long conditioned his more bullish predictions about AI on the technology being allowed to proliferate freely throughout the economy. His comments on Monday suggest he is less confident about the prospects of that happening.

His argument is rooted in an economic phenomenon known as “Baumol’s cost disease,” which states that as technological advances make some goods and services cheaper to produce, goods and services that are less susceptible to productivity gains become relatively more expensive. This means that rapid technological progress in certain industries could leave Americans devoting an ever-larger share of their incomes to industries that have barely changed.

Fed chairman Warsh reportedly did not respond directly to the comments on Monday, describing AI as a “hinge point for the U.S. economy” and concluding that he is “cautiously optimistic.”

Before taking office, Warsh argued that AI could be a disinflationary force that increases productivity and justifies lower interest rates.

#10381. What is Model Routing in AI?

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

"Do you know the closest ATM?" and "I was charged twice, the refund never arrived, and now my card is blocked" are both customer messages. Most AI apps send both to the same large model and pay large-model prices for each one.

Model routing fixes that. A router looks at each request and sends it to the cheapest model that can handle it, and keeps the expensive model for the requests that need it.

In this guide we'll cover what model routing is, how routers decide, and what it saves. Then we'll build a small router in about 60 lines of JavaScript and run it over 200 customer messages. At one setting it matched a large model's accuracy for about a third of the cost. At another it came within a point and a half for 89% less.

Model routing in AI is the practice of sending each request to the model best suited to it, instead of sending every request to one model. A router sits between your app and a pool of models, reads each request, and picks a model based on what you care about: cost, speed, or quality.

You'll also see it called AI model routing, LLM routing, or LLM model routing. They all mean the same thing. The pool might be a small and a large model from one provider, or models from several providers behind one API.

The idea rests on one observation: most requests are easy. A small model answers them as well as a large one, in a fraction of the time and for a fraction of the price. The router's whole job is finding the hard ones.

The diagram below shows a typical AI model routing architecture.

Model routing works in three steps: the router reads the request, decides which model should answer it, and forwards the request to that model. The middle step is where routers differ. Routing tools decide which model to use in one of four ways.

Rule-based routing uses rules you write by hand. Requests from free-plan users go to a small model. Anything tagged as code goes to a coding model. Prompts over a certain length go to a model with a bigger context window. It's simple, predictable, and free to run, but the rules only know what you thought of in advance.

Intelligent model routing uses a model to make the decision. A small, fast classifier reads each request and predicts which model in the pool will answer it well. You'll also see it called smart or dynamic model routing.

Two more terms come up here. Task-aware routing picks a model by the kind of job, like summarising, coding, or answering a support question. Context-aware routing also looks at what surrounds the request, like the conversation so far, the user, or the tools available.

The big platforms work this way. Microsoft describes its Foundry model router as "a trained language model" that picks a model for each prompt in real time. Google says Gemini Notebook uses its new Decisions API as a real-time router, serving everyday queries with up to 40% lower latency. I've tested the Google Decisions API against Jev on the same messages we'll use below.

Cascade routing tries the cheapest model first and only moves up when the answer isn't good enough. The usual test is confidence: if the cheap model is sure, keep its answer. If it isn't, send the request to a stronger model. It's also called confidence-based routing, and it's what we'll build below.

A cascade needs no separate classifier, because the first model's own confidence does the routing. The trade-off is that escalated requests pay for two models and wait for both.

Fallback routing is about staying up, not saving money. If a model times out, hits a rate limit, or its provider has an outage, the router sends the request to the next model on a list. Most production routers combine fallbacks with one of the three methods above.

The main benefits of model routing in AI systems are lower cost, faster responses, and fewer outages, without giving up quality on the hard requests.

We'll build a cascade router for a job every support tool has: sorting customer messages. Each message gets one of ten labels, like atm support or request refund.

The test set is 200 messages from Banking77, a public set of banking support messages: ten labels, 20 messages each. They're the same 200 messages from my zero shot classification test, which is where the single-model numbers below come from.

Put both keys in a .env file and run the examples with node --env-file=.env. It's the same setup as in my guide to getting a YouTube API key.

Create router.mjs. The first function sends the message to Jev with one multiple-choice question, and returns the label Jev picked along with its confidence:

Confidence runs from 0 to 1. When nearly all the probability sits on one label, it's close to 1. When Jev is torn between two labels, it drops.

The second function asks Claude Opus 5.5 the same question. The output_config block limits the answer to one of our labels, so there's no free text to parse. SitePoint's guide to LLM structured output with JSON Schema explains how that works.

The router itself is about a dozen lines:

If Jev is at least 80% confident, its answer goes straight back. If not, Claude answers instead. And if Claude fails, the router falls back to Jev's answer, because a shaky answer beats an error page.

Try it on an easy message and a harder one:

Jev was sure about the lost card. On the ATM question it leaned towards card acceptance with a confidence of 0.64, so the router asked Claude, which got it right.

Because cheap, strong, and threshold are options, the same function routes between any two models.

Model routing reduces AI costs by keeping easy requests on a cheap model and paying for the expensive one only when it's needed. Here's what that looked like on our 200 messages, starting with each model on its own:

Opus gets six more messages right out of 200, and costs more than 120 times as much.

Now the router, at four confidence thresholds:

Speed improved too. At the 0.8 threshold, the messages Jev kept came back in a median of 227 ms. The ones that escalated took about 2.1 seconds, because they waited for both models.

A note on method: I ran every message through both models once and saved the answers, then replayed the router over them at each threshold. That's how you compare thresholds without paying for the same test four times.

Then I ran the router live to check. At 0.95 it scored the same 95.0% and sent 61 messages to Opus. At 0.8 it scored 93.5% and sent 20, a point under the replay. Two answers moved: one of Jev's confidence scores landed at 0.82 instead of 0.78, just over the line, and Opus changed its answer on one message. Scores near the threshold shift a little between runs, so leave yourself a margin.

The choice of cheap model matters less than you'd think. With Google's Gemini Decision 1 in first place instead of Jev, a 0.7 threshold reached the same 95% for US$0.28 per 1,000 messages.

Model routing can cost a little quality, and the threshold decides how much. In our test the gap to Opus ranged from nothing at 0.95 to two points at 0.7.

The loss comes from one place: answers the cheap model got wrong while feeling sure. At the 0.8 threshold, Jev kept five wrong answers because its confidence was above the line. Opus got four of those five wrong as well, so only one was a real loss: "Do all ATMs take this card?", which Jev filed under card acceptance with a confidence of 0.91.

Escalating isn't risk-free either. On one message, Jev had the right label with a confidence of 0.44, and Opus overruled it with the wrong one.

To optimize costs using AI model routing, measure first, route second, and keep measuring. These six steps cover LLM model routing cost optimization for any pair of models:

The return is easy to estimate once you know the split. If nine in ten requests stay on a model that costs 1% as much, the bill drops by about 89%, which is what we measured.

Several inference providers have multi-model routing built in, and most AI gateway platforms support model routing too, so you don't have to write your own. As of November 2026, these are the top model routing solutions for AI apps. Each name links to the tool's model routing docs:

Hosted model routing platforms for large language models decide for you, which is the fastest way to start. A hand-built router like ours takes more work, but you choose the signal and you can see why every request went where it did.

An LLM router is the component that does model routing for large language models. It can be a function in your own code, like the one in this guide, a hosted model such as Microsoft Foundry's model router, or a feature of an AI gateway.

Smart model routing is another name for intelligent model routing: a model, not a hand-written rule, decides where each request goes. Dynamic model routing means the same thing.

The ROI of AI model routing depends on how much of your traffic a cheaper model can handle. In our test, a 0.8 threshold kept 89.5% of messages on the cheap model and cut the cost per 1,000 messages from US$1.96 to US$0.22, for about a point of accuracy. The build was about 60 lines of code.

OpenRouter's auto model routing works through its Auto Router. You set the model to openrouter/auto, and a decision model picks a model and a reasoning effort for each request. You pay the standard rate of whichever model it selects, with no extra fee.

OpenClaw model routing is a primary model plus an ordered list of fallbacks. In the OpenClaw model routing configuration you set agents.defaults.model.primary and agents.defaults.model.fallbacks, and an agent can override the fallback list. When a model fails, OpenClaw first rotates auth profiles on the same provider, then moves to the next model on the list, as its model failover docs describe. That makes it fallback routing, not cost-based routing.

An AI gateway simplifies model routing by putting every model behind one API, one set of keys, and one place for logs. Your app calls the gateway, and the routing rules live in config instead of code, so changing a model doesn't need a deploy.

Mid-stream failover is when a router switches models after a streamed response has already started, because the first model failed partway through. It's the hardest kind of failover, because the user has already seen part of an answer. Many routers only fail over before the first token arrives and return an error after that, so check what your gateway does.

#10380. These viral ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ details have fans even more hyped for the game’s release

After a brutal 13-year wait, the next entry in the Grand Theft Auto franchise is finally just a day away from release—and somehow, the hype is still growing.

Grand Theft Auto VI expands the series’ formula of letting players run rampant through near-perfect parodies of real cities. This time, Miami, Florida, is represented as Vice City, Leonida, where players will have more options than ever before when it comes to both criminal escapades and the minutiae of everyday life.

Reviews are starting to roll in—almost entirely glowing reviews, mind you—and early players are sharing the juicy details of their adventures in Vice City.

A vibrant, living world

While GTA VI’s main characters and story (a criminal couple named Jason and Lucia striving to find a happy ending together) are a major draw for some, it’s the random strangers around them that are driving the last wave of viral anticipation for the game.

Take one encounter described in Jason Schreier’s review for Bloomberg. While cruising around Vice City, Schreier saw a delivery truck rear-end a sedan, then speed away. He rescued the sedan driver from his vehicle as it caught on fire, then watched as the man decided to re-enter the burning car to increase his injuries with the goal of a bigger lawsuit payout. Schreier had the choice to blackmail the man or help his case as a witness. He chose the second option and received a few thousand bucks of the settlement via BuckMe, the game’s version of Venmo.

That degree of detail is all over GTA VI, Schreier wrote, with other side encounters including busting a parrot-smuggling operation inside a liquor store and helping free caged apes after an animal rights protest. His review has garnered more than 2.6 million views on social media, just one of several reviews from major outlets singing the game’s praises and leaving fans counting down the hours until midnight.

“This review has put tears in my eyes, I’m so buzzing,” one user wrote. 

“How can you even fathom this level of immersion,” asked another.

Radio realness

The GTA franchise has always been known for both its humor and its realism, and no feature exemplifies that more in GTA VI than its radio stations.

The in-game radio includes a stacked list of pop hits by the likes of Ariana Grande, Billie Eilish, Rihanna, and PinkPantheress—the latter of whom appears in the game herself as a radio host, much to the delight of her fans. 

Other radio offerings include true crime podcasts, news stations, and advertisements full of pitch-perfect satire of American and Floridian culture. “Have you always dreamed of abusing your power without consequence?” asks one in-game ad that’s already gone viral. “Well, now you can, when you join the Vice City Police Department.”

Days’ worth of gameplay

After more than a decade of anticipation, no one wants their GTA VI playthrough to be a short-lived experience. Luckily, that’s far from the case.

GTA VI’s main story takes around 70 hours to complete on average, according to a sample of players who ran the game for IGN. That included 115 hours on the high end and 42 hours on the low end, which the reviewer admitted was a rushed playthrough. Another reviewer said that even their 70-hour playthrough was a bit rushed, and they’ve since played another 30 hours with plenty of content still to discover.

Grand Theft Auto VI officially releases tomorrow, November 19, on the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S. Check out the launch trailer below.
