#10355. Automating Contract Signing in Node.js: Webhooks, Verification, and Storing Signed PDFs

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sending a document for signature is the easy part of an e-signature integration. One POST request and the signer gets an email. The work that actually breaks in production happens afterwards: knowing when the document was signed, trusting the notification that told you so, handling the same notification twice, and getting the final PDF into storage before the download link expires.

This tutorial builds that whole loop in Node.js with Express. An event in your app (a deal is approved, a client is onboarded, a task moves to "ready to sign") sends a contract from a template. When the signer finishes, a webhook arrives, your server verifies it, and the signed PDF plus its audit trail get saved without anyone touching them.

The code uses Firma.dev, the e-signature API I work on, because I needed a real API to make the examples runnable. The patterns are not specific to it, though. Signature verification, idempotent handlers, short-lived download URLs, and reconciliation jobs show up in almost every webhook-driven integration, and the same structure applies whether you're receiving events from a payment processor, a CI system, or another signing provider.

There's a fifth part that tutorials usually skip: a reconciliation job that catches anything the webhooks missed. We'll build that too, because webhooks are a notification mechanism, not a delivery guarantee.

Before sending anything, wrap the HTTP calls in one place. This is where authentication lives, and it's also where you handle 429 Too Many Requests once instead of in every caller. Most APIs, this one included, return a Retry-After header on a 429, so the client should honour it rather than guessing a backoff.

The 503 branch matters later. When a document has just been completed, the final PDF and its completion certificate take a moment to generate, and the download endpoint says so with a 503 and a Retry-After instead of handing you a half-built file.

The trigger depends on your product. It might be a route handler, a queue consumer, or a CRM automation calling into your service. What matters is that the function doing the sending is small and takes plain data:

Two design choices are worth calling out.

Use a single create-and-send call when you can. Many signing APIs split this into "create a draft" and "send the draft." That's useful when a human needs to review the document first, but for automation it creates a window where your process can crash between the two calls and leave an orphaned draft. A combined endpoint makes the operation atomic from your side.

Store the provider's ID on your own record immediately. Webhook payloads reference the signing request, not your deal or customer. Without that mapping you'll end up searching by email address, which falls apart as soon as one client signs two documents.

Here's the first place integrations quietly go wrong. Webhook signatures are computed over the exact bytes the sender transmitted. If Express parses the body as JSON first, you lose those bytes, and re-serialising the object won't reproduce them (key order, whitespace, and number formatting can all change). Signature checks then fail intermittently, which is the worst kind of failure.

The fix is to use express.raw() on the webhook route only, so the handler receives a Buffer:

Most webhook providers sign payloads with HMAC-SHA256 using a shared secret. The details vary, so read your provider's docs for the exact header format, but the scheme here is common: the header looks like t=1731456000,v1=5f2b..., and the signed string is the timestamp, a dot, and the raw body. Stripe uses a very similar format, and the Standard Webhooks spec describes the same idea as a vendor-neutral convention.

Each line here defends against something specific.

The OWASP guidance on cryptographic storage covers the other half of this: the secret belongs in an environment variable or secrets manager, never in the repository.

Every serious webhook system delivers at least once, not exactly once. If your endpoint is slow, returns a 5xx, or the network drops the response, the sender retries. Firma.dev, for example, makes up to three attempts per event (immediately, then after at least five minutes, then after at least an hour) and treats anything other than a 2xx as a failure, including redirects. Other providers retry more aggressively. Either way, your handler will eventually see the same event twice.

The defence is to record each event's unique ID and skip ones you've seen. In the server above that's alreadyProcessed and markProcessed. For a demo, a Set works:

In production, use your database and let a unique constraint do the work, so two concurrent deliveries can't both pass the check:

Also notice the order in the route: respond with 200, then do the work. Many providers time out deliveries after a few seconds (five, in this case). Downloading a PDF and uploading it to object storage can easily take longer than that, and a timeout counts as a failure, which triggers a retry, which triggers duplicate work. Acknowledging fast and processing asynchronously avoids that loop.

setImmediate is fine for a tutorial, but it has a real weakness: if the process dies after sending the 200 and before finishing the work, the event is acknowledged and lost. In production, push the event onto a durable queue (BullMQ, SQS, a jobs table) before responding. Step 7 covers the safety net for whatever still slips through.

Now the actual business logic. You'll usually see several event types (sent, viewed, a signer signed, declined, expired, completed). Only one of them means "the document is final":

Three things in here are easy to get wrong.

Don't treat "a signer signed" as "the document is done." With multiple signers, each one triggers its own event, and a per-signer "all complete" flag can be true on more than one of them. Key your storage logic off the single completion event.

Don't persist the download URL. Pre-signed URLs expire (this one carries an expires_at). Saving the link to your database and serving it to users later produces broken links a few minutes or hours later. Download the bytes and store them in storage you control. Swapping the fs.writeFile calls for an S3 PutObject or a Google Drive upload is a drop-in change.

Store the audit trail, not just the PDF. If a signature is ever disputed, the PDF shows what was signed, and the audit trail shows who signed it, when, and from where (timestamps, IP addresses, the sequence of views and signatures). That evidence is what makes an electronic signature defensible, which brings us to the legal side.

Retries are finite. Endpoints go down during deploys. Some providers auto-disable a webhook after enough consecutive failures, and events aren't guaranteed to arrive in order. Any one of these can leave a completed document sitting unsaved.

A small scheduled job closes that gap. Keep a list of signing requests your app considers "pending," and periodically ask the API for their real status:

Since storeSignedDocument overwrites by ID, running it twice for the same document is harmless. That's the property you want from every step in a webhook pipeline: doing it again shouldn't change the result.

None of this is legal advice, but a few facts shape how you build.

In the US, the ESIGN Act and the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (adopted by 49 states) give electronic signatures the same legal standing as handwritten ones for most commercial documents. ESIGN also has requirements around consumer consent and record retention, which is part of why you store the final PDF yourself rather than relying on a third-party link.

In the EU, eIDAS defines three levels: simple (SES), advanced (AdES), and qualified (QES). SES and AdES cover most business contracts. QES requires a qualified trust service provider and certificate-based identity, and some documents (certain property transfers and court filings, depending on the country) require it or exclude e-signatures entirely. Check which level your document types need before you pick a provider, since not every API offers every level.

Across jurisdictions, the evidence that holds up is the same: who signed, how they were identified, when it happened, and proof the document hasn't changed since. That's the audit trail and the completion certificate, which is why Step 6 stores both.

If you're evaluating providers for a workflow like this, the questions that matter at the integration level are mostly not on the pricing page:

The send call is one line. The reliability comes from everything around it: keeping the raw body for verification, checking timestamps and comparing in constant time, acknowledging fast and deduplicating by event ID, downloading files before their links expire, and running a reconciliation job for the events that never arrive. Get those right and contract signing becomes something your app does in the background, with no one chasing signatures or copying PDFs between folders.

For the Firma.dev-specific details used here (event names, header format, rate limits), see the webhooks guide.

#10354. HBO Max is moving ahead with an Elon Musk documentary despite his $1B investment. Here’s why

Skydance CEO David Ellison says the company will honor the distribution deal to stream Alex Gibney’s Musk documentary, even after Elon Musk’s $1 billion investment in the company.

The nearly four-hour documentary on the Tesla and SpaceX executive is expected to hit HBO Max in early 2027, but Musk’s recent investment had put into question whether the streamer would air it.

HBO is now part of Skydance following the controversial merger between Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount earlier this year. While Bleecker Street Media holds the U.S. theatrical rights and Universal Pictures the international distribution rights, HBO has the North American streaming rights for the documentary.

When asked about the potential conflict at the 2026 DealBook summit in New York on Wednesday, Ellison told New York Times columnist and DealBook founder Andrew Ross Sorkin that he intends to follow through with the commitment to A24.

“We believe in independence. We don’t believe in censorship of any kind,” Ellison told Sorkin. He added: “We have that deal with A24, and of course we’ll honor it.” 

According to Deadline, Ellison appears to have misattributed the deal to HBO’s pay-1 deal with A24, a multiyear licensing deal that gives HBO exclusive streaming rights to A24-made films. A pay-1 deal gives a premium cable network or streaming service the first window to exclusively air a film following its theatrical release. Pay-1 windows often last about 18 months, at which point other networks can acquire streaming rights.

Deadline reports that the deal Ellison refers to is most likely a commitment with HBO Documentary Films instead.

The statement from Ellison follows Musk’s own criticism of the documentary, which he referred to as a “hit piece.”

The documentary in question features interviews with figures from Musk’s life, including his first wife, Justine Musk; Tesla cofounder Martin Eberhard; and Ashley St. Clair, the mother of Musk’s 13th child. Additionally, figures from the entrepreneur and tech world are also featured in the film, including LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman and British Canadian computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton, also known as the “godfather of AI.”

Ellison also took the stage to praise Musk, calling him “the greatest entrepreneur of our time.”

He added: “To have his vote of confidence and to have him as a shareholder is an honor and a privilege. And if there was any opportunity to be able to collaborate with him in the future, from our perspective, it would be a privilege.”

#10351. ANT stock update: Anthropic share price, stock trading time, and more for Claude maker’s much-hyped IPO

It’s almost here: Anthropic is expected to go public on Thursday, November 19, and its IPO share price has been set well above the company’s target range, a sign that demand for the stock is strong.

The AI giant, best known for its LLM Claude, is in the middle of the biggest—or at least the most-hyped—initial public offering since SpaceX went public in a record stock listing earlier this year. 

Late Wednesday, Anthropic confirmed that it priced shares at $83, above earlier estimates of $70 to $78 per share.

Anthropic’s offering consists of 980 million shares of Class A common stock, with the company selling roughly 956.4 million shares itself and certain stockholders selling about 23.6 million.

The Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg, and other media outlets reported the $83 share price earlier in the day.

A lot is hinging on how well Anthropic’s stock performs in the public markets on Thursday as AI-related stocks have seen a significant pullback in the wake of escalating “AI bubble” fears compounded by the recent ouster of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang.

Here’s what to know as Anthropic’s stock is about to commence trading.

About Anthropic

Anthropic, PBC (Nasdaq: ANT) is an artificial intelligence public benefit corporation based in San Francisco. It was established in January 2021 by a group of seven cofounders who left now-rival OpenAI over safety and direction concerns and disagreements. 

That includes Dario Amodei, CEO; Daniela Amodei, president; Tom Brown, chief compute officer; Jack Clark, head of public benefit; Jared Kaplan, chief science officer; Sam McCandlish, chief architect; and Chris Olah, interpretability research lead.

Anthropic’s primary product is its Claude LLM, which itself has multiple tiers, and other features such as its AI assistant, its coding tool Claude Code, and more. 

What’s particularly notable about Anthropic’s IPO is that it may be considered one of the first and most valuable pure-play AI IPOs—meaning that Anthropic’s primary function and market is AI, while many other companies in the space (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, etc.) have broader business operations that include AI.

Also notable is the company’s prospectus, which includes more than 90 pages of risk factors that investors should take into consideration. That list, it’s worth pointing out, also includes “existential risks” to humanity.

When is Anthropic’s IPO?

Anthropic shares are expected to start trading on November 19, when the stock market opens at 9:30 a.m. ET.

The stock will trade under the ticker “ANT,” which was already at the top of Yahoo’s trending stock tickers list on Wednesday, despite not actively trading yet.

A countdown clock on the ANT ticker page alerts users to when trading is expected to begin—down to the second (although the actual time may differ).

Anthropic shares will trade on the Nasdaq Global Select Market.

What is the IPO share price of ANT?

The initial public offering price for ANT shares is $83, higher than Anthropic’s projected range of $70 to $78 per share.

How many ANT shares are available in its IPO?

Anthropic’s initial public offering will include the sale of 980 million shares of its Class A common stock, above an earlier estimate of 825 million.

The lead underwriters for Anthropic’s IPO are Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, per its prospectus.

How much is Anthropic expected to raise in its IPO?

Anthropic’s valuation is now as high as $1.5 trillion, Bloomberg estimates.

That puts it on the cusp of the top 10 largest companies in the world by market capitalization; it could be worth more than Walmart and Berkshire Hathaway, for instance, and roughly on par with Tesla and Meta. 

Assuming it does reach a valuation of $1.5 trillion, Anthropic would be one of 15 public companies worth at least $1 trillion. 

What are analysts saying?

As noted, Anthropic is the biggest pure-play AI IPO to come along, which has investors chomping at the bit. But it’s also rife with risks, as outlined in its prospectus and filing statements. 

The company is definitely driving revenue: Its S-1 filing shows that through the first nine months of 2026, Anthropic saw revenue of $33.2 billion, up more than 1,200% year over year.

Analysts generally have a rosy view of the stock ahead of the IPO. New Street Research rated it a “buy,” and analyst Pierre Ferragu called it a “generational IPO,” according to CNBC.

KGI Securities likewise rated the stock as “buy,” and gave it a price target of $105, significantly higher than the pre-IPO range. Analysts at Morningstar set a target of $92 per share, also seeing the stock as “undervalued” ahead of trading.

Disclosure: Morningstar was founded by Fast Company’s owner, Joe Mansueto. This developing story has been updated.

#10350. Nvidia claims its Vera CPU can gain up to 39% performance boost via software optimization at SC26 — architectural fine-tuning is needed to fully unleash custom Olympus cores

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Reviews, benchmarks, and updates on current GPUs.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

Vera can speed up old code out of the box, but there's more performance to unlock

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nvidia's Vera CPU, designed as both a standalone data-center part and a host for Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 servers, offers impressive performance thanks to substantially higher execution resources per core than its predecessor, Grace. However, Nvidia admits at Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) that existing software cannot always take full advantage of Vera's resources without adaptation for the architecture.

The company shared that architecture-specific software optimizations can boost Vera's performance by nearly 39% in certain computationally intensive workloads. But despite offering unbeatable single-thread performance, the CPU is not positioned for general-purpose workloads.

Get the full Tom's Hardware experience on your device with our brand-new app. Bookmark articles, use our smart search feature, personalize your feed, and get push notifications so you never miss a beat.

Unlike Grace, which relies on off-the-shelf Neoverse V2 CPU cores developed by Arm, Vera uses Nvidia's proprietary Olympus cores specifically designed to maximize per-core performance as well as to ensure high aggregate throughput. To that end, Nvidia equipped Olympus with a wide front end that features a 10-wide decoder, a neural branch predictor, a deep out-of-order execution engine, six vector execution units, four load pipelines, two store pipelines, all backed with large private caches and advanced prefetch mechanisms.

In fact, Nvidia deliberately opted for 88 high-performance general-purpose cores with support for its proprietary spatial multithreading technology (176 threads in total) rather than maximizing the number of cores per socket, as the maximum possible single-thread performance was one of the key design goals for Vera.

"CPU design is really just a game of trade-offs," said Hannah Coutand, who leads Vera CPU marketing at Nvidia, in an interview with Tom's Hardware Premium. "You could maximize for a lot of cores, but literally when you maximize the die for lots of cores, you do not actually have space to maximize for IPC, like instructions per clock."

Although Nvidia primarily positions Vera as a CPU for agentic AI and other AI-related workloads, the company originally conceived its Olympus microarchitecture with data processing applications in mind. As it turned out, the key attributes of Vera — high per-core performance, high memory bandwidth, and low memory access latency — are precisely what agentic AI workloads need as well, according to Coutand.

"We are very clear in our strategy with Vera and our positioning with Vera that it is not a general-purpose CPU," Coutand said. " If you want a web server for your cloud data center, there are probably other choices that are better suited for that than Vera. [Vera is made for] workloads […] that require that high per-core speed, high memory bandwidth, low latency. […] It has great fungibility for lots of workloads as long as those workloads value the things that Vera is good for."

To assess the computational capabilities of Nvidia's custom Olympus microarchitecture and its advantages over Neoverse V2, Nvidia's researchers used a double-precision general matrix multiplication (DGEMM) workload based on an assembly kernel from OpenBLAS, an open-source linear algebra library. While OpenBLAS features a kernel tailored for the Arm Neoverse V2 cores that power Nvidia's Grace processor, it lacks one specifically designed for Olympus.

To examine the efficiency of the two microarchitectures, the researchers used a standalone benchmark called miniKernelGEMM with a 128 × 128 matrix multiplication problem that fits into the L1 cache of both processors.

The Grace CPU achieved 4.51 instructions per clock (IPC) and 13.03 FP64 operations per cycle with the Neoverse V2 kernel, whereas Vera executed 5.43 instructions per clock and 15.69 FP64 operations per cycle with the very same code, an improvement of approximately 20%.

However, when the researchers used a kernel specifically optimized for Olympus, Vera’s performance increased to 7.53 instructions per clock and 21.75 FP64 operations per cycle. As a result, Vera outperformed its predecessor by nearly 67% on a per-core, per-clock basis in this particular workload.

Grace's Neoverse V2 microarchitecture has four 128-bit SIMD pipelines that can perform a total of 16 FP64 operations per clock, whereas Nvidia's Olympus has six such pipelines that can execute up to 24 FP64 operations per cycle, a 50% improvement.

But where the Neoverse V2-optimized kernel uses 81.4% of Grace's peak FP64 throughput, it uses only about 66.5% of Vera's computational capabilities. With changes to matrix tile organization, register allocation, and instruction scheduling that better suit the Olympus microarchitecture, the researchers managed to utilize 90.6% of its peak FP64 throughput, according to Nvidia's tutorial published at SC26.

While software developed and optimized for existing Arm-based data center processors can still benefit from the capabilities of Nvidia's Olympus cores without any specific optimizations, the company's SC26 benchmark results demonstrate that at least some applications will need to be fine-tuned for the new microarchitecture to take full advantage of its execution resources. Of course, it remains to be seen how much performance can be gained through Olympus-specific optimizations in workloads other than matrix multiplication.

As Nvidia expands beyond CPUs that primarily serve as companions to its data center GPUs and chases the standalone server CPU market, the company will have to ensure that performance-critical software takes advantage of the architectural peculiarities of its processors, much like Intel and AMD have done for decades.

But the company is already deeply experienced with partner and ecosystem development for platforms like CUDA, so as Vera is more widely adopted, that experience could prove useful in spurring optimizations for these CPUs going forward.

Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

#10349. Replit’s CEO on its stunning turnaround, ‘AI psychosis,’ and the risk Silicon Valley is ignoring

A couple of years ago, Replit was flatlining at a few million dollars in annual revenue and running a mostly empty office after a layoff. Today the vibe coding pioneer is valued at $9 billion, up from $3 billion just six months ago. CEO Amjad Masad reveals what made the turnaround possible. Masad also weighs in on what he calls “AI psychosis,” and says cybersecurity, not AI extinction, is the risk worth focusing on.

This is an abridged transcript of an interview from Rapid Response, recorded live at Masters of Scale Summit 2026 and hosted by former Fast Company editor-in-chief Robert Safian. From the team behind the Masters of Scale podcast, Rapid Response features candid conversations with today’s top business leaders navigating real-time challenges. Subscribe to Rapid Response wherever you get your podcasts to ensure you never miss an episode.

The growth you’ve seen has been extraordinary. From the inside, what does that feel like? Is it exhilarating when everything is growing so fast? Is it terrifying? Do you have to pinch yourself to say, “Is this real?”

It’s all of the above. The first feeling I had was a little bit of vindication, because I started talking about everyone being able to code and create software back in 2010, when I was building the kind of precursor to Replit as an open-source project. Then I was a founding engineer at Codecademy, where we taught a lot of people to code. And when we started Replit in 2016, we were like, “We want to blur this distinction between learning to code and doing code, and build an environment that really makes it so that anyone with an idea can build software.” And for a long time, people didn’t believe us. Raising capital was hard. Recruiting people was hard.

Because some of the technology wasn’t ready yet.

It wasn’t ready. It was on track, and I could see it happening. There were many moments where the company could have died, or I could have quit. It would have been very easy to quit at many different moments. And so in 2024, when we invented what would later be called vibe coding, when we came up with the first fully natural-language-based programming environment, there was nothing out there at the time. People really appreciated it, and we started seeing these stories of people having ideas.

One of the early experiences I had was someone recording a video of themselves and posting it on Twitter and YouTube where they were crying because they had this idea of overlaying all their memories and their photos on a map and being able to explore their life through this map. It’s a simple idea, but it’s a personal app. It’s not even a commercial app. And he was crying because he said he had this idea for so long. He tried to do it with all these different technologies, and for the first time, he was able to do it.

I’ve also been an angel investor for a while, and I’ve seen some early AI companies do the hypergrowth and the hyper-deceleration within a year. So there’s a fair amount of paranoia built into how we operate.

You immigrated to the U.S. in 2012, and as you say, you spent years grinding away as you were trying to find your groove. Are there lessons from those slower times that you go back to as a leader in the midst of the noise you’re in now?

Yeah. There were many moments where it felt darkest just before we were able to invent something big or new. Even just before we invented agentic coding in 2024, we had to do a layoff. We were six or seven years into the company, we had 2 or 3 million in ARR, and it was flatlining. It wasn’t growing at all.

Two or three million?

Yeah.

Two or three million, just a couple of years ago. Now you’re at a billion.

Yeah.

I want to pause and acknowledge that. That’s crazy, man.

It is wild. And we were burning a ton of money. We hired a great team, but the future hadn’t arrived as fast as I thought it would. So I kind of mistimed it a little bit. Unfortunately, we had to do a layoff. Around the same time, we also upgraded the office. We went from a small office in SF to this really massive office in Foster City because the space was so cheap there. It was this big office, but it felt dark and cold because it wasn’t really occupied. Every day, I would go into the office and sit at my desk and wait for another person to quit.

The thing about doing a layoff is you also burst a bubble. You burst a dream. I’m sure a lot of people are familiar with Steve Jobs’s reality distortion field. Really, every founder needs to create some reality distortion. You’re selling a dream, and suddenly you’re saying, “We’re running out of money.” The dream immediately dissipates.

I know you’re a believer that the idea of vibe coding is great, that everyone could be able to code. And you can code in natural language. I’m curious: Among your own team, you’ve got engineers who are building a product that essentially can make their job obsolete in some ways.

There’s somewhat of an inherent tension inside the company, for sure. Some of our engineers are motivated by that. You’d be surprised. We have a few AI engineers who joined the team saying, “I want to automate my job.” It’s like, “What kind of motivation is that? Do you hate coding? Is that why?”

But everyone inside is really excited by the impact we’re having on people’s lives, like the entrepreneurs we’re seeing build businesses that otherwise wouldn’t have been built because they suddenly have that power. That’s really what gets us excited. I do think we all face this question. Every knowledge worker essentially faces this question of, “The things that I’m doing might lead to my replacement,” because you’re generating data that is getting trained in the AI models, and that tension exists in tech broadly.

In the tech neighborhood, you’ve decried what you call “AI psychosis.” You’ve called out Dario Amodei specifically at Anthropic for overheated predictions about AI-fed job losses. Today’s fear over AI agents run amok, is that also psychosis? Or is that a different AI risk?

No. In fact, that is really the thing I’ve been talking about, the risk I’ve been talking about. I’ve been on the cybersecurity risk for two years now. I think everything else is a distraction from that. When they go out and talk about how AI is conscious, and they go meet the Pope and do all this random stuff, it’s really distracting, and it’s also, in many ways, destructive and bad for humanity for us to care about the well-being of these machines when we haven’t really figured out the well-being of humans.

It also distracts from the real question of cybersecurity. Just in the past two or three days, we’ve had major platforms being hacked. And if you’re not paying attention, if you’re running an enterprise and you’re not paying attention to this stuff, if you’re running a company on some of these platforms that are insecure, you’re putting your business and your users at risk. I don’t think the world has taken that seriously. It’s a disaster brewing. The Hugging Face incident was the first kind of shot on that, but it’s not the end.

This week has been pretty brutal for cybersecurity. Our team is working nonstop. Overnight, everyone’s in the office making sure we’re mitigating whatever vulnerabilities are coming up. It’s a very serious moment for the world, and the talk about AI extinction is just not relevant right now. We need to focus on cybersecurity.

#10346. 4 places where cutting AI costs is a mistake

Every leader says the same thing when they roll out a new AI tool. “Give it to our employees, let them run!” What actually happens three months later is that access gets capped, usage gets metered, and exploration gets restricted to the people with the most seniority.

What happened? A scarcity mindset took hold, driven by the assumption that controlling costs means restricting employees’ access to tools.

Here are the four places a scarcity mindset shows up most frequently, and what you can do about it.

1. Metering access like a utility bill

Companies like Tesla, Uber, and Meta have started to cap spending. Tesla, for example, now limits employees to $200 per week. On paper, that sounds reasonable. But for developers who have built these tools into their daily work, hitting the limit doesn’t magically make their deadlines or responsibilities disappear.

Instead, developers are forced to make a decision. Do they use the assistance now to improve their work, or save it for a harder assignment later? This kind of metering is the equivalent of telling employees that their laptop batteries last just one hour and can be charged only once a day.

The far better way to control costs is to match the tool to the task. While it’s easy to reach for the most powerful model every single time, think of it like renting a car for your next trip to the grocery store. A Ferrari costs far more than a Toyota, and doesn’t make any material difference in terms of getting your groceries home. Likewise, a routine coding task doesn’t need the most expensive artificial intelligence model to produce an excellent result.

There are now tools that automatically route coding tasks to models capable of doing them well at a lower cost. Employees should be able to focus on the work without having to choose a model or calculate the cost of every request.

2. Keeping up with the Joneses

Companies often default to using whatever tool the rest of the market has already crowned the winner, without evaluating whether it actually fits the job. Using a popular model feels like the safe, defensible choice, and if everyone else is using it (the thinking goes), then you can’t get blamed for choosing it, too. Safe, maybe, but not smart.

A better option is to focus on finding the tool that will get you the outcome you want as efficiently as possible.

One note: Data matters here too. Before anyone pastes company information into a tool, leaders should know how the provider stores it, whether it can be used for training a model, and how the contract actually protects your information.

3. Sticking with what worked 10 years ago

A tech leader I spoke with recently argued that some tasks are better handled by conventional software than by AI, especially when they follow fixed rules and must produce the same result every single time given the same inputs. Fair enough. You don’t need a language model to calculate 1+1=2.

But consider this. An investor recently gave me blunter advice. You either swim against the current and probably will not make it, or you move faster by swimming with the current. Opting out of AI is not an option, because competitors who adopt it will outpace those who don’t. Rationing the chance to try something new is how you end up behind. So give developers room to test a better way, then judge whether the results justify changing the process.

4. Limiting exploration to senior staff only

This pitfall is extremely common and leaders should avoid it by all means. Junior team members often have the freshest instincts for a new tool, and they’re the ones kept from experimenting, on the assumption that only senior staff can be trusted to test things out. Give every developer room to keep trying, testing and learning, regardless of seniority.

Leaders can make the freedom to experiment feel safer by setting clear boundaries around which data, systems, and websites each tool can access.

The costume of prudence

All four of these behaviors come from a scarcity mindset wearing the costume of prudence. For leaders who recognize their own organization in any of this, the place to start is simple. Think about your own laptop, and whether you would accept being told you could only use it one hour a day. That is what metering access feels like to the people doing the work, whether they are developers or not.

Teams already know the difference between a leader who trusts them with power and one who doles it out. Which one are you?

#10345. Preventing API Contract Drift in TypeScript Applications

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A frontend application can compile successfully and still fail when it communicates with the backend.

Imagine a backend developer changes an API response from:

The backend works correctly. The frontend also builds without errors. However, a component expecting user.name now receives undefined.

This is an example of API contract drift: the frontend and backend no longer agree on the structure or behavior of an API.

The problem becomes more difficult when several developers or teams work on different parts of an application. A change made by one team may affect another team's assumptions without producing an obvious error during development.

TypeScript helps catch many programming mistakes, but its types do not automatically validate data received over HTTP. A type declaration can describe what the application expects without proving that the server actually returns it.

In this tutorial, we'll look at a practical way to make API contracts more reliable.

Consider a typical frontend API function:

The function promises to return a User, so TypeScript allows the application to access properties such as name and email.

The return value of response.json() is not automatically checked against the User interface. The interface only provides compile-time information; it does not validate the actual JSON received from the server.

the frontend may still treat the response as a User even though the data has a different structure.

This is particularly important when working with:

Independently deployed frontend and backend applications.

APIs maintained by different engineering teams.

The solution is to validate data at the boundary where it enters the application.

Zod is a TypeScript-first schema validation library. It allows developers to describe expected data structures and validate actual values against those definitions.

Now create a schema for the user response:

First, UserSchema describes the structure that the application expects at runtime.

Second, z.infer generates the corresponding TypeScript type from the schema.

This means developers do not need to maintain a separate interface and validation definition for the same data structure.

The response is initially treated as unknown, which prevents the application from assuming that untrusted data already has the expected structure.

UserSchema.parse() validates the actual response.

If the backend returns an unexpected property type or misses a required field, Zod throws a validation error instead of allowing invalid data to move silently through the application.

You can also use safeParse() when you prefer to handle validation errors without exceptions:

This approach is useful when API responses are external or when a frontend must provide more controlled error handling.

One common mistake is placing API validation logic directly inside React components.

For a small application, this may seem convenient. As the project grows, however, it becomes difficult to reuse validation rules and identify where data transformations happen.

A better approach is to separate API schemas, service functions, and UI components.

The responsibilities are straightforward:

schemas/user.ts defines the expected user data.

api/client.ts handles common HTTP configuration.

api/users.ts contains user-related API requests.

hooks/useUser.ts manages data fetching for React.

components/UserProfile.tsx displays the validated data.

This structure makes it easier to change an API implementation without rewriting the UI.

It also makes testing more manageable because validation logic can be tested independently of React rendering.

For more ideas on organizing application code, see SitePoint's guide to modern JavaScript modules.

Runtime validation protects an application when data arrives. However, teams also need a shared description of what an API is supposed to accept and return.

OpenAPI provides a standard format for describing HTTP APIs, including:

For example, an endpoint can be described using an OpenAPI document:

This document describes what the endpoint should return.

Both frontend and backend developers can refer to the same contract instead of relying on separate assumptions or outdated documentation.

Swagger Editor helps developers write and validate OpenAPI documents. It also provides a convenient way to inspect API definitions.

Swagger UI turns an OpenAPI document into interactive API documentation, allowing developers to explore endpoints and test requests.

Redoc provides another way to generate readable API documentation from an OpenAPI specification.

These tools are particularly useful when APIs are maintained by multiple developers or consumed by several applications.

Maintaining API types manually across frontend and backend repositories creates opportunities for inconsistencies.

For example, a backend developer might add a new optional property while the frontend continues using an older interface.

One way to reduce this duplication is to generate TypeScript definitions and API clients from an OpenAPI specification.

Orval is a useful tool for this workflow.

It can generate TypeScript clients and types from an OpenAPI document, helping frontend developers work with consistent endpoint definitions.

A typical configuration might look like this:

The exact configuration depends on the Orval version and the structure of the OpenAPI document.

Once configured, the client can be regenerated when the API specification changes.

This reduces the amount of repetitive code developers need to maintain manually.

However, generated types should not be confused with runtime validation. They improve consistency during development, but an application may still need to validate responses received from external systems or services that cannot be fully trusted.

Frontend developers often need to build or test features before the corresponding backend endpoint is ready.

Waiting for a complete backend implementation can slow down development, particularly when multiple teams work independently.

Mock Service Worker (MSW) helps solve this problem by intercepting network requests and returning controlled responses.

You can define a mock handler for the user endpoint:

The frontend can now make normal HTTP requests while MSW supplies predictable responses during development or testing.

You can also simulate an invalid response:

This makes it possible to check whether the application's validation and error-handling logic behave as expected.

MSW is particularly valuable because it allows frontend tests to run without requiring a live backend environment.

Runtime validation and generated clients improve reliability, but they do not automatically guarantee that independently developed services remain compatible.

For systems with multiple services, contract testing can provide another layer of protection.

Pact is a contract-testing tool that allows consumers and providers to verify their expectations about API interactions.

Consider a frontend application that expects the user endpoint to return:

The consumer defines the expected interaction.

The backend provider can then run verification against that contract to check whether its actual response satisfies the consumer's expectations.

This helps identify breaking changes before they reach production.

These tools solve different problems. A project does not necessarily need all of them, but larger applications can benefit from combining the approaches that match their architecture.

A contract is only useful if developers consistently check it when making changes.

A practical approach is to run validation and tests automatically whenever someone opens a pull request.

For example, a GitHub Actions workflow might look like this:

The api:validate script should be configured to validate the project's OpenAPI document or run the relevant contract checks.

The test command should execute the application's automated tests.

For a production project, you may also want to include:

The objective is to detect incompatible changes before they are merged.

A failed pipeline gives developers an opportunity to investigate the change while the context is still fresh.

API contracts become harder to maintain when several teams contribute to the same system.

For example, a company might have separate teams responsible for:

If nobody owns an API contract, small changes can create unexpected problems for other teams.

Assigning clear ownership helps establish who reviews changes, maintains documentation, and coordinates breaking updates.

This becomes particularly important when an organization expands its engineering capacity across locations or adds several specialized teams. Companies planning that kind of growth may also need to consider enterprise IT recruitment as part of their wider engineering workforce strategy.

Regardless of how a team is assembled, its development process should establish clear responsibilities for API design, versioning, testing, and release coordination.

A few practical conventions can make a significant difference:

Assign an owner to every important API or service.

Document breaking changes before implementation.

Require contract-related tests in pull requests.

Keep generated clients synchronized with the API specification.

Communicate deprecations before removing existing fields.

Monitor production errors after deploying API changes.

These practices help prevent a growing engineering organization from becoming a collection of disconnected services.

API contract drift is not simply a TypeScript problem. It is a coordination problem that becomes visible when applications and services develop different expectations about the same data.

TypeScript provides useful compile-time checks, but it cannot guarantee that an HTTP response matches a declared interface.

A more reliable approach combines several techniques:

Use OpenAPI to document API expectations.

Generate TypeScript clients with tools such as Orval.

Use MSW to test frontend behavior without a live backend.

Use Pact when consumer-provider contract verification is appropriate.

Run validation and tests automatically in CI/CD.

You do not need to introduce every tool at once. Start by validating external API responses, document important endpoints, and gradually automate contract checks as the application grows.

The result is a codebase where developers can make changes with greater confidence and where frontend and backend teams have a shared understanding of how their systems communicate.

Upgrading a PC right now may be a non-starter, but you can still improve someone's overall desk experience without spending a lot.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It’s a tough time for PC gamers and enthusiasts. Graphics cards are scarce, RAM and storage are prohibitively expensive, and the PC port of GTA VI isn’t expected until sometime in 2027 at the earliest. But core components aside, there are plenty of other ways to improve someone's PC PC-related experience, and upgrading their desk space is a good place to start looking. We’ve already covered key peripherals, like keyboards and gaming accessories, so below we’ll be focusing on desk devices that let you connect more devices, stay more organized, improve comfort, or just keep things cleaner. From some of the best desk-friendly PC speakers I’ve tested to tactile media and software controls, and a monitor riser that integrates a USB hub and charging, there’s something here to improve everyone’s desk experience. I own most of these devices, or similar previous-gen versions that are no longer available, and can attest to their usefulness. Some live on my desk at the office, while others are better suited for home PC setups, but they all make for a better experience when I'm at my desk.

These unique wrist and elbow rests are designed to hang over the edge of your desk, making them great for those who lean on their elbows, or just for a cramped desk setup. Available in multiple colors and sizes, the 11.8-inch version I have is wide enough that I only need to use one for my compact keyboard at work. So I use the other one at home for my gaming setup.

If your phone has magnetic wireless Qi charging, there's no nicer, more convenient way to charge it than a stand like this, especially when there's additional power and ports for other devices. This Anker model has a built-in retractable cable that can handle up to 60W, so you can charge a non-gaming laptop with this stand at the same time as your phone. I've used a similar charging stand for years, and it helps keep things clean while making charging a second device as simple as grabbing the pull-out cable.

With 11 ports and up to 10 Gbps speed, a solid aluminum shell, and buttons so you can cut power to individual ports, this USB hub is a great addition to a desk without enough ports. It has external power for better stability, and even a 20W USB-C PD port on the end for charging phones or peripherals.

Just plug this simple device into a USB port, and you can control the volume and select tracks without reaching for your keyboard or mouse. It supports recent Windows versions, as well as Mac, without the need for a driver.

The Stream Deck Mini features six configurable buttons for launching software or controlling devices. It's compatible with the full suite of Stream Deck tools from Elgato. There are cheaper alternatives, but the ecosystem (supporting software as well as lights and smart devices) makes these devices more versatile than the competition.

This quirky device combines an under-desk headphone hook and a 20W PD USB charger with one USB-C and two USB-A ports. It brings a bit of extra convenience and tidiness to your desk setup. It comes in four colors and I've been using one under my standing desk since 2023.

These speakers are some of the best desk-friendly options we've tested, with great sound, lots of connection options, and excellent build quality. They're a great audio upgrade to most desk setups, and I have a pair that I bought in 2012 that still look and sound as good as they did when they were new.

We've all dealt with a crumb-covered desk or a dusty PC at some point. This all-in-one desk vacuum and portable air blower can tackle both those issues, and much more. Connect the included accessories to one end for blowing, and the other for suction. It's lived near my desk for years, and my main complaint is that Hoto doesn't ship with a wall mount or a good way to hold its many accessories. I solved that issue with my 3D printer.

This compact 1920 x 720 IPS monitor supports touch input and a 75 Hz refresh. I wouldn't recommend actually playing games on it, but it's a great second screen for game or work chats (or whatever else you want to keep a close eye on while doing other things). Its 24:9 aspect ratio (and a built-in kickstand) make it a good fit under your primary desktop monitor. It also costs less than competing name-brand alternatives.

You can think of this monitor stand as a sort of all-in-one desk upgrade. It packs a USB hub, 15W Qi charging, a 20W PD charging hub, built-in storage drawers, and a metal frame that has space for up to two 32-inch monitors. That's a lot of functionality in one device. I've owned a previous version of this stand since 2020. In fact, it's currently holding the monitor I'm looking at as I type this, and I've found it a good fit for my cramped office desk, since it helps keeps things tidy.

After a rough start with the Mattel Aquarius as a child, Matt built his first PC in the late 1990s and ventured into mild PC modding in the early 2000s. He’s spent the last 15 years covering emerging technology for Smithsonian, Popular Science, and Consumer Reports, while testing components and PCs for Computer Shopper, PCMag and Digital Trends.

#10340. You can now Email and Text (via Google Messages, iMessage) with Gemini

As previewed at I/O 2026, you can text — via Google Messages and iMessage — or email directly with Gemini.

Instead of using the Gemini app, you can now reach the AI assistant to “start tasks and get updates” using your preferred method of communication. To get started, go to gemini.google.com/channels.

You can now assign Gemini ‘tasks’ for free in six countries

Text with Gemini works via Google Messages and iMessage. Google does note that this method is “not end-to-end encrypted and may be accessible by your carrier.” The setup process involves verifying a phone number. Existing numbers associated with your Google Account appear automatically, and there’s the ability to add a new one.

Afterward, you’ll receive a text from Gemini via RCS Business Messaging that offers a pretty straightforward chat experience. Before sending, booking, or other “major actions,” Gemini will ask for 1-tap confirmation.

…you can text a request, snap a photo of a school flyer to add dates to your Google Calendar, or get scheduled check-ins in a private 1:1 thread. If your plans change while Gemini is working, simply reply to the text to steer the task mid-run without starting over.

(Amusingly, Text with Gemini coexists with the existing Google Messages integration, which you can distinguish by the old blue/purple icon.)

Email with Gemini lets you “start tasks and get updates by emailing” gemini@google.com. Google explicitly names Gmail, Apple Mail, or Outlook as supported clients, while emails from Gemini are always “1:1 to you (never “Reply-All”) with a link to review and confirm your results.”

Forward a batch of school emails to add key dates to Google Calendar, spot schedule conflicts, or send over threads and PDFs to sort out medical bills and track insurance renewals.

You can manage phone numbers and turn off both options from this new Channels page. If you’re more familiar with using your email client or phone’s messaging app, Text and Email with Gemini might boost your assistant usage. This is available first in the US.

Meanwhile, when announced in May, these two options were intended for Gemini Spark, which has since been integrated into the main Gemini experience as “tasks.”

Nvidia is stuck between a rock and a hard place, as "irreplaceable talent" wants to leave if Jensen Huang isn't reinstated as CEO amidst the spy affair controversy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Following the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang, there are warnings that important Nvidia employees are planning to leave if the company doesn’t reinstate him. According to the Wall Street Journal, an employee sent an internal letter to the top executives and board of directors stating that “failure to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive could lead to the loss of ‘irreplaceable talent.’” Huang resigned last week amidst a firestorm of reports about an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, a further affair with VP of health care Kimberly Powell, and allegations the former relationship may have facilitated chip smuggling into China.

According to WSJ’s sources, director of developer technology Nader Khalil wrote the letter, urging that Huang be reinstated as CEO, lest the company lose loyal and important employees. The letter’s recipients, according to WSJ, comprised roughly 60 direct reports and the 10 members of the board, and Khalil warned that “Irreplaceable talent at Nvidia is now contemplating departing.”

The internal letter, along with the standwithjensen.com open letter to reinstate him, shows how important Huang is to the employees of Nvidia. Without the key long-term employees, which the company heavily depends on, progress could halt, or possibly regress, as Nvidia would lose the employees who have worked on and built the architectures and systems that make Nvidia what it is, along with their leader, Huang — who has recently stated that he would be honored to come back as CEO.

The open letter, signed by multiple Nvidia current and former employees, and tech CEOs and investors, states that employees are concerned that Huang was ousted unfairly and without due process, expressing that the employees do not have “access to the board’s private deliberations,” and that they have not been shown evidence that Alice Huang was indeed a spy, which even US intelligence doesn’t have solid evidence of. The open letter demands that Huang be reinstated as CEO while ensuring an independent investigation and a fair hearing, including providing a “specific, evidence-based explanation” of why Nvidia shouldn’t keep Huang as CEO — with Huang scheduled to appear before a House of Foreign Affairs panel concerning his affairs with the alleged spy.

Despite the letter, the support of other Silicon Valley CEOs, and even President Trump, Nvidia is still not considering bringing Huang back as CEO. Nvidia is the hottest AI hardware company at the moment, and its employees are highly desirable not only within the US, but possibly China as well. China surely wouldn’t mind getting its hands on a few key employees, who, if they choose to leave, are likely not going to have a hard time finding another job.

#10338. Google AI Mode rolling out temporary threads

Following last week’s Gemini 4 Hydrogen launch, a small update to AI Mode today lets you start a “temporary thread” that won’t be saved to your Google history.

Like in the Gemini app, anything you discuss in a temporary thread isn’t saved to your account. It won’t appear in conversation history or influence future recommendations.

These AI Mode responses won’t be personalized with past preferences. After you close a temporary thread, there’s no way to access it again.

To launch, tap the new pen button with a dotted border in the top-right corner, which is the same icon used in the Gemini app. The personalized greeting at the top of the prompt box switches to “Welcome, stranger.”

This is an alternative to opening google.com in Incognito Mode, while still being able to use the model picker. Meanwhile, Google’s use of “threads” to describe AI Mode conversations versus “chats” in the Gemini app is interesting.

Temporary threads are rolling out globally starting today on mobile and desktop browsers across all AI Mode languages.

This joins other changes that Google is still testing for AI Mode. With the latest Google app beta on Android, you can now quickly upload from Google Drive, which joins Gallery, Camera, and Files as attachment options. You can also now access Canvas on Android.

#10336. 10 Best AI App Builders I've Used in 2026 (and What Each One Gets Wrong)

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI App Builders are exploding in popularity, and for good reason. It’s never been easier to build real, functional apps and internal tools using app builders. To test them all, I built the same app on 10 of the most popular AI app builders and tested each across usability, cost, correctness, and ease of use. Most of them can turn a paragraph of description into something that looks like software within a single session. The differences show up around the tenth prompt, when you learn what each edit costs and who has to fix the code once something breaks. I took every price from the vendor's own pricing page on October 29, 2026.

TLDR: Of the best AI app builders I've used, Softr is the one I'd hand to a team that needs auth, data, user groups or integrations. The other nine I tested include code generators such as Lovable and Bolt and visual platforms such as Bubble and Glide, and each one carries a cost or upkeep trade-off worth seeing before you commit.

I looked at the same seven things in every tool, from the first prompt onward:

Softr gets used a lot by operations and business teams as their AI app builder for secure client portals, internal tools and other business apps, none of which require code. Write a short brief in your own words, and the AI Co-Builder turns it into a database plus the core app that sits on it: tables, pages and layouts, the data connections behind them, plus user groups and permissions, so real users can sign in from day one. Workflows come as the next step, either by prompting the Co-Builder again or by adding them in the visual editor.

The Free plan is $0 for unlimited apps, with room for 5 app users, 3 builders, 5,000 records and 5 AI credits each month. Basic runs $19 per month, Pro $99 and Business $329, all on annual billing. Enterprise pricing is custom and includes SSO and SCIM for organizations managing access at scale. The full plan table sits on Softr's pricing page.

Lovable builds full-stack web apps through conversation, writing React code while it takes care of hosting, SSL and the backend. It's designed to move a founder or product team from a prompt to a shareable prototype, and the preview updates as the agent works.

Base44 calls itself a no-code AI platform: you explain the app, and it generates the structure, design and logic while running the backend itself. Authentication, a database and analytics come on every plan, Free included.

Base44 is free for 25 message credits a month. Starter costs $16 per month and Builder $40 per month, both on annual billing, with Pro at $80 and Elite at $160.

Bolt is a coding agent that writes full-stack projects in the browser and runs them on Bolt Cloud, which supplies hosting, databases and integrations. It suits people who want to watch the code take shape and edit it themselves.

Bolt Free is $0 with 1M tokens a month and Bolt branding. Pro costs $25 per month with 10M tokens, and Teams runs $30 a month for each member on monthly billing.

Replit pairs its Agent with a cloud workspace, so a description turns into a running app whose sign-in, database, hosting and monitoring come wired up. The homepage pitches it to people who don't code, though the result underneath is a code project.

Core costs $20 per month ($18 with annual billing) and Pro costs $100 per month ($90 with annual billing). Enterprise is custom and adds SSO, SCIM and audit logs.

Glide starts internal business apps from whatever you hand it, whether a spreadsheet, a written prompt or a PDF, and its newer platform, GlideOS, reads a sheet's structure and relationships to draft screens and workflows. Its apps grew up on phones, and that heritage still shapes the product.

Glide Free is $0 with limited credits. Basic costs $25 per month, Plus $50 per month and Pro $125 per month; annual billing isn't offered yet, according to Glide.

Bubble Free gives you 50K workload units and 500 AI credits each month. Web plans run $32 per month for Starter, $119 for Growth and $349 for Team, all on annual billing.

Retool is an internal tools engine aimed at engineering teams. You describe or assemble an app that connects straight to production databases, APIs and LLMs, with auth and access controls in place at deployment.

v0 generates full-stack Next.js web apps from a prompt and deploys them to Vercel, with Design Mode for visual tweaks and GitHub sync for the code. It's designed around a developer's workflow.

v0's Free plan gives new users $5 of one-time credits and caps messages at 7 per day. Plus runs $30 a month per user, and Business $100 a month per user.

Figma Make turns prompts and Figma design context into code-backed prototypes and web apps you can publish at a URL. It can also scaffold a Payload backend with a database, APIs, auth and an admin panel, or connect to Supabase for sign-in and stored data.

Figma's Starter plan is free with up to 500 AI credits a month. Figma lists a Professional Full seat at $16 per month with 3,000 AI credits, and Organization Full seats cost $55 per month on annual billing.

Collins Dictionary named "vibe coding" its Word of the Year for 2025, and the phrase now covers any workflow where you describe software in plain language and an AI produces it. AI app builders package that workflow with hosting, data and sign-in, so a non-developer can get from idea to something clickable without installing anything.

The questions buyers ask have turned plainer since then: what each edit costs, who keeps the app running, and whether a client can sign in and see their own records alone. A generated front end makes a good demo, and a team using it every day needs permissions and a predictable bill for the next hundred edits.

Softr is now my default when recommending AI app builders. It handles teams, auth, and real company data better than any other product. The AI Co-Builder drafts tables, pages and user groups, workflows follow as the next step, and the app keeps running on maintained platform components with no codebase to patch. App-user pricing and an editor that works without AI credits keep later changes from turning into a running meter.

Three situations call for a different tool. Glide makes a better mobile-first choice when the app spends its days on phones in the field. Bubble gives more front-end design freedom when a project calls for bespoke layouts, interactive animation or heavy brand styling. If your engineers want version control and audit logs and can handle a technical setup, Retool covers that need.

Agents are moving inside the apps these tools produce. Gartner expects task-specific AI agents inside 40% of enterprise applications by the close of 2026, against under 5% in 2025, so a 2027 app builder will need to host agents that respect the same permissions as human users.

Building is also leaving the builder's own window. The Model Context Protocol now sits under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation and reports more than 97 million SDK downloads a month, with client support in ChatGPT and Claude, among others. Softr's changelog dates its official Claude and ChatGPT connector to October 6, 2026, and I expect more teams to start an app from the chat assistant they already use.

The caution comes from Gartner too: it predicts organizations will scrap upward of 40% of agentic AI projects before 2028, citing escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Going into 2027, I'd judge any builder on whether it keeps agent costs and access rules visible to the team running the app.

Neville Naidoo is a technology journalist covering AI, startups, and the digital economy, with a focus on how emerging technologies are constantly evolving and shaping our everyday life.
